evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Commercial Classes & Utilization
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: U.S. wheat is divided into five commercial classes: Hard Red Winter (~40% of production), Hard Red Spring (~25%), Soft Red Winter (~15-20%), White wheat (10-15%), and Durum (~3-5%). HRW and HRS dominate bread flour; SRW dominates cakes/pastries/crackers; White dominates noodles/flatbreads.
evidence_registry.source_title: Wheat Sector at a Glance
evidence_registry.citation_location: Wheat Classes and End Uses Section
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: The United States produces five major classes of wheat... Hard Red Winter (HRW) accounts for about 40 percent of total production... Hard Red Spring (HRS) accounts for about 25 percent of production and is valued for high protein... Soft Red Winter (SRW) accounts for 15-20 percent... White wheat accounts for 10-15 percent...
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: National economic survey and crop reporting statistics.
evidence_registry.limitations: Annual class percentage shares vary with weather, plantings, and relative price incentives.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Vernalization & Photoperiod Genetics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter wheat carries functional VRN2 repressor and recessive vrn-A1/vrn-B1/vrn-D1 alleles, requiring 4-8 weeks of cold chilling (0-7°C) to induce VRN1 and downregulate VRN2. Spring wheat carries dominant mutations/deletions in VRN1 promoter or intron 1 (or loss of VRN2), conferring constitutive VRN1 expression without chilling.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of California Davis / Molecular Genetics and Genomics
evidence_registry.source_title: The vernalization gene VRN1 in wheat and barley encodes a MADS-box transcription factor
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Fu, D., Szűcs, P., Yan, L., Simpson, P.R., Sanfilippo, P., Sherman, J.D., Belcram, H., Dubcovsky, J.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Differences between winter and spring growth habits in polyploid wheat are controlled mainly by allelic variation at the VRN-1 loci (Vrn-A1, Vrn-B1, and Vrn-D1)... Deletions within the promoter or the first intron result in dominant spring alleles that bypass the requirement of vernalization for flowering.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Peer-reviewed molecular cloning and genetic mapping across hexaploid and diploid wheat germplasm.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cultivar-specific chilling durations depend on specific homoeoallelic combinations (e.g. Vrn-A1 vs Vrn-B1 vs Vrn-D1).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Base Temperature & GDD Calculation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: The standard thermal base temperature (Tbase) for wheat phenology modeling is 0.0°C (32.0°F). GDD is calculated as ((Tmax + Tmin)/2) - Tbase. McMaster and Wilhelm demonstrate that Method 1 (resetting daily mean to Tbase if < Tbase) and Method 2 (resetting individual Tmax/Tmin to Tbase if < Tbase) can diverge by up to 83% in cold seasons.
evidence_registry.source_title: Growing degree-days: one equation, two interpretations
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: For wheat, base temperature is frequently taken as 0°C. When daily minimum temperature drops below 0°C, the two common interpretations of the GDD equation result in accumulated thermal time discrepancies exceeding 50% in winter/early spring environments.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Evaluation of temperature records and crop modeling routines across Northern and Central Great Plains.
evidence_registry.limitations: Agro-meteorological modeling standard; models must explicitly specify whether Method 1 or Method 2 is applied.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Thermal Time Accumulation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Hard red spring wheat requires approximately 1,150-1,400 GDD (°C, base 0°C) or 2,100-2,500 GDD (°F, base 32°F) from seeding to physiological maturity. Emergence requires ~100-140 GDD (°C); jointing occurs at ~400-500 GDD (°C); heading occurs at ~750-900 GDD (°C).
evidence_registry.source_organization: North Dakota State University Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Use of Growing-Degree Days to Determine Spring Wheat Growth Stages
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Bauer, A., Fanning, C., Enz, J.W., Eberlein, C.V.
evidence_registry.citation_location: NDSU Extension Bulletin EB-37, Tables 1-3, pp. 1-8
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cumulative growing-degree days (base 32°F) required to reach developmental stages in hard red spring wheat: emergence ~180-250 GDD-F; 4-leaf/tillering ~450 GDD-F; jointing ~800-900 GDD-F; heading ~1400-1600 GDD-F; ripe ~2100-2400 GDD-F.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (ND, MN, SD, MT)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Measured in field plots across North Dakota. Calculated using base 32°F (0°C).
evidence_registry.limitations: Photoperiod sensitivity and planting date can shift GDD requirements by +/- 10-15%.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Winter Wheat Growth Staging & Phenology
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter wheat progresses through Feekes 1-3 (emergence, tillering; fall ~400-600 GDD-C), winter dormancy, Feekes 4-5 (green-up, pseudo-stem erection; ~150-250 GDD-C post-dormancy), Feekes 6 (first node/jointing; critical herbicide/grazing cutoff), Feekes 10.5 (anthesis/flowering; ~500-650 GDD-C post-jointing), and Feekes 11.4 (ripe; ~600-800 GDD-C post-anthesis). Total spring thermal time: ~1,300-1,750 GDD-C (base 0°C).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Wheat Growth and Development
evidence_registry.citation_location: Publication MF3300, Visual Chart and Technical Narrative
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Feekes scale staging for winter wheat: Feekes 1 to 5 occur from emergence through greenup. Jointing (Feekes 6) occurs when the first node is visible above the soil surface. Booting (Feekes 10), heading (Feekes 10.1-10.5), and grain fill (Feekes 11.1-11.4). First hollow stem occurs just prior to Feekes 6.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard agronomic staging guide calibrated for Great Plains winter wheat production.
evidence_registry.limitations: Calendar days per stage depend strongly on spring temperatures and moisture availability.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Effective Water Extraction Depth (Generic Mature Wheat Baseline)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: USDA-NRCS NEH Part 652 Table 3-4 lists 4.0 to 5.0 ft (1.2 to 1.5 m) for mature wheat in deep, well-drained unrestricted soils. This represents the effective water extraction depth (~80% available soil water extraction zone), NOT maximum physiological root penetration, and does not distinguish winter wheat from spring wheat.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook, Part 652 (Irrigation Guide), Chapter 3: Crops
evidence_registry.citation_location: Chapter 3, Table 3-4 ('Depths to which the roots of mature crops will extract available soil water from a deep, uniform, well drained soil under average unrestricted conditions'), p. 3-8
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Table 3-4 lists effective rooting depth for mature crops grown in deep, well-drained soils under irrigation: Wheat: 4.0 - 6.0 ft (1.2 - 1.8 m).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep, well-drained, non-compacted soils without shallow bedrock, hardpans, or shallow water tables.
evidence_registry.limitations: Generic wheat entry; represents effective water extraction depth (~80% zone), NOT maximum root penetration. Soil compaction, claypans, or fragipans restrict active rooting to 60-90 cm.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Seasonal Water Use & Peak ETc (Winter Wheat)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal crop water use (ETc) for winter wheat in the Central Plains ranges from 15 to 25 inches (380 to 635 mm), with typical benchmark trials averaging 17.7 to 23.4 inches (450 to 600 mm). Peak daily water use occurs during heading through grain fill, averaging 0.30 to 0.35 inches/day (7.6 to 8.9 mm/day), with single-day evaporative demand reaching 0.40 to 0.54 inches/day under hot, windy conditions.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Agricultural Crop Water Use
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Winter wheat total seasonal water use typically ranges from 15.4 to 23.4 inches under Kansas conditions... Peak daily water use rate averages 0.30 to 0.35 inches per day during the boot to flower stages.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains (Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas High Plains)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Hard red winter wheat under dryland and irrigated systems
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Calculated from lysimeter and neutron probe soil water balance measurements.
evidence_registry.limitations: In dryland systems without irrigation, actual ET is bounded by precipitation and available stored subsoil water.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Seasonal Water Use & Root Zone (Spring Wheat)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Hard red spring wheat requires 12 to 16 inches (305 to 406 mm) of seasonal water (ETc) to reach full yield potential, extending to 16-18 inches (400-450 mm) under high-yield irrigation. Active root zone depth spans 42 to 48 inches (107 to 122 cm), with effective managed extraction focused in the top 36 inches (91 cm). Water use averages ~1.5 inches per Haun stage between 8-leaf and kernel hard maturity.
evidence_registry.source_organization: North Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station / USDA-ARS Northern Great Plains Research Laboratory
evidence_registry.source_title: Soil water use by plant development stage of spring and winter wheat
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Bauer, A., Black, A.L., Frank, A.B.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Experiment Station Bulletin No. 519, Tables 4-7, pp. 8-16
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cumulative seasonal evapotranspiration for spring wheat ranged from 12.2 to 15.8 inches across trials. Spring wheat extracted water to depths of 48 inches, with 80% of extraction occurring in the upper 3 feet. Daily water use peaked between heading and milk stage.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (North Dakota, South Dakota, Eastern Montana, Western Minnesota)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field lysimeter and gravimetric/neutron probe trials at Mandan, ND.
evidence_registry.limitations: Water use efficiency decreases under severe high temperature stress during late grain filling.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Nutrient Removal Rates & Seed Safety
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Per bushel of harvested wheat grain (60 lb): removal is 0.50 lb P2O5/bu and 0.25 lb K2O/bu. If wheat straw is baled and removed: removal is 3.7 lb P2O5 per dry ton and 29.0 lb K2O per dry ton. In-furrow fertilizer applied directly with drilled wheat seed must not exceed 100 lb/acre total fertilizer salts (N + P2O5 + K2O) and must not exceed 10 lb N/acre as urea to avoid seedling salt/ammonia injury.
evidence_registry.source_organization: The Ohio State University, Purdue University, Michigan State University Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations for Corn, Soybean, Wheat, and Alfalfa
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Culman, S., Fulford, A., Camberato, J., Steinke, K.
evidence_registry.citation_location: OSU Extension Bulletin 974, Table 17 (p. 25), Table 21 (p. 31), and Starter Placement (p. 38)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Nutrient removal per unit of yield: Wheat grain removes 0.50 lb P2O5/bu and 0.25 lb K2O/bu. Wheat straw removes 3.7 lb P2O5/ton and 29 lb K2O/ton. Seed-placed fertilizer: Do not apply more than 100 lb/acre total plant nutrients (N + P2O5 + K2O) with the seed; do not apply more than 10 lb N/acre as urea.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Midwest and Eastern Corn Belt (OH, IN, MI, IL, MO)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Modern soft red winter wheat and general wheat cultivars
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard tri-state agronomic field calibrations updated for contemporary cultivars.
evidence_registry.limitations: High-protein hard wheats (e.g. 14% HRS) export slightly more nitrogen per bushel than lower-protein SRW.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Nitrogen Fertility & Protein Target
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Spring wheat nitrogen recommendations in the Northern Plains use an economic optimal N approach targeting maximum net return rather than maximum yield. Grain protein benchmark is 14.0% to prevent market dockage. N recommendations require a 0- to 24-inch profile soil nitrate-N test, subtracting residual nitrate-N and previous crop credits from total regional N needs. Base N need ranges from 2.2 to 2.5 lb total available N per bushel in western ND to 2.0-2.2 lb N/bu in eastern ND.
evidence_registry.source_title: Fertilizing Hard Red Spring Wheat and Durum
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: The optimal N rate for spring wheat depends on the cost of N, the price of wheat, and regional yield response data... Total available N includes fertilizer N, soil test nitrate-N to a 2-foot depth, and previous crop N credits... Aiming for 14.0% protein avoids discounts.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Montana)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Calibrated across 15+ years of N-response trials in eastern, western, and Langdon regions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excessive N increases risk of lodging and lodging-induced foliar diseases without increasing yield.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Winter Wheat Fertility & Soil Test Interpretation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Kansas winter wheat total nitrogen requirement is calculated as 2.4 lb N per bushel of realistic yield goal. Net fertilizer N is calculated by subtracting 0- to 24-inch profile nitrate-N, organic matter mineralization credit (10-20 lb N per % OM depending on region), and previous crop credits. Soil test phosphorus critical level is 20 ppm (Bray P-1 or Mehlich-3); potassium critical level is 130 ppm exchangeable K.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Soil Test Interpretations and Fertilizer Recommendations
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Ruiz Diaz, D.A., Leikam, D.F., Lamond, R.E., Mengel, D.B.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Publication MF2586, Wheat Nitrogen & Phosphorus Equations, pp. 6-10
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Wheat N recommendation formula: Nrec = (Yield Goal x 2.4) - Profile Nitrate-N - Previous Crop N credit - (Soil OM% x 10). If profile sample is not taken, default profile credit is 30 lb N/acre. Critical P is 20 ppm.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains (Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Nebraska)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard K-State Soil Testing Lab calibration curves for grain-only winter wheat.
evidence_registry.limitations: Dual-purpose graze-and-grain systems require an additional 30-40 lb N/acre to support fall/winter forage production.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Residue Biomass & C:N Ratio
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat straw has a typical carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of approximately 80:1 (range 60:1 to 100:1). Semi-dwarf wheat has a harvest index (HI) of 0.40 to 0.48, generating ~1.0 to 1.3 lb of straw residue per pound of grain (~60-80 lb residue per bushel). A 60 bu/acre grain yield produces 3,600-4,800 lb/acre dry residue. Because the C:N ratio far exceeds the microbial threshold of ~24:1, decomposition causes temporary soil inorganic N immobilization.
evidence_registry.source_organization: USDA-NRCS East National Technology Support Center
evidence_registry.source_title: Carbon to Nitrogen Ratios in Cropping Systems
evidence_registry.citation_location: Soil Quality Technical Note No. 1, Table 1 & Narrative, pp. 1-3
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Table 1 shows typical C:N ratios: Wheat straw is 80:1. The ideal microbial diet is 24:1. High C:N residues (>24:1) decompose slowly and cause microorganisms to scavenge and temporarily immobilize available mineral nitrogen.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Wheat straw and small grain residues
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard USDA-NRCS soil health and nutrient management technical guidance.
evidence_registry.limitations: Actual straw C:N varies with nitrogen fertility and drought stress at maturity.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Freeze Injury Thresholds (Winter Wheat)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Freeze sensitivity in winter wheat increases dramatically as plants de-harden in spring: Tillering (Feekes 4-5): 12°F (-11.1°C) for 2 hours causes leaf chlorosis/burn; Jointing (Feekes 6-8): 24°F (-4.4°C) for 2 hours causes growing point mortality and stem splitting; Boot (Feekes 10): 28°F (-2.2°C) for 2 hours causes head entrapment and floret sterility; Heading/Flowering (Feekes 10.5): 30°F (-1.1°C) for 2 hours kills male flower parts (anthers), causing complete floret sterility.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Spring Freeze Injury to Kansas Wheat
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Shroyer, J.P., Mikesell, M.E., Paulsen, G.M.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Table 1: Temperatures that cause freeze injury to winter wheat at various stages of development: Tillering: 12°F for 2 hours; Jointing: 24°F for 2 hours; Boot: 28°F for 2 hours; Heading: 30°F for 2 hours; Flowering: 30°F for 2 hours.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Thresholds represent approximately 2 hours of exposure at plant canopy level.
evidence_registry.limitations: Soil moisture, topography, and canopy density can buffer or exacerbate canopy air temperatures.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Wheat Cardinal Temperatures
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Comprehensive review of cardinal temperatures for wheat: Vegetative development: Tbase = 0.0°C, Topt = 20.3°C, Tmax = 32.7°C. Anthesis (flowering): Tbase = 9.5°C, Topt = 21.0°C (range 19-22°C), Tmax = 31.0°C. Grain filling: Tbase = 9.2°C, Topt = 20.7°C (range 18-22°C), Tmax = 35.4°C. Temperatures >31°C during anthesis impair microsporogenesis and induce sterility; temperatures >35°C during grain filling deactivate starch synthase.
evidence_registry.source_organization: European Journal of Agronomy / Agricultural and Forest Meteorology
evidence_registry.source_title: Temperatures and the growth and development of wheat: a review
evidence_registry.citation_location: Eur. J. Agron. 10(1):23-36 / Agric. For. Meteorol. 97(1):73-93, Table 2 & Table 4
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Base, optimum, and maximum cardinal temperatures across wheat developmental phases. Anthesis: Topt 21.0°C, Tmax 31.0°C. Grain filling: Topt 20.7°C, Tmax 35.4°C. Exceeding Tmax halts dry matter accumulation.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Meta-analysis of over 80 published controlled-environment and field temperature response studies.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cardinal temperatures represent steady-state physiological responses; short episodic heat shocks have dynamic thresholds.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Empirical Heat Stress Yield Threshold (Winter Wheat)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Statistical analysis of 25 years of Kansas winter wheat variety performance trials identified a critical extreme heat threshold of 34°C during spring growth. Degree days accumulated above 34°C caused severe, non-linear yield reductions, whereas exposure between 15°C and 34°C was neutral or beneficial. Negative impacts of warming on winter wheat yields substantially outweighed benefits from reduced severe winter freezing.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University / University of Arkansas
evidence_registry.source_title: Effect of warming temperatures on US wheat yields
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Tack, J., Barkley, A., Nalley, L.L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: We find a sharp threshold at 34°C: exposure to temperatures above this point causes severe yield losses in Kansas winter wheat... An increase in extreme heat degree days above 34°C reduces yield more than exposure to moderate warming increases it.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Central Great Plains (Kansas winter wheat production)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Hard red winter wheat cultivars (variety trial callset)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Econometric piece-wise regression linking variety trial yields to gridded daily temperature data.
evidence_registry.limitations: Empirical yield response threshold from historical Kansas data; should not be interpreted as a universal biological survival ceiling.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Heat Stress at Anthesis & Grain Filling
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Daytime temperatures >= 31-35°C during anthesis (especially 5 days pre-anthesis through flowering) cause severe pollen sterility, impaired pollen tube elongation, and floret abortion, drastically reducing grain number per spike. High temperatures (>= 32-35°C) during grain filling accelerate leaf senescence, shorten the grain-filling period, and reduce thousand-kernel weight (TKW) by up to 5% per 1°C increase above 20°C.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Department of Agronomy
evidence_registry.source_title: Impact of high temperature stress on floret fertility and individual kernel weight of wheat
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Prasad, P.V.V., Pisipati, S.R., Ristic, Z., Bukovnik, U., Fritz, A.K.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: High temperature stress (>31°C) during flowering significantly decreased floret fertility, kernel number per spike, and harvest index... Post-anthesis high temperature decreased individual kernel weight and shortened grain filling duration.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Controlled environment and field chamber temperature experiments at K-State.
evidence_registry.limitations: Nighttime temperatures exacerbate daytime heat stress; elevated night temp (>= 20-24°C) increases dark respiration and carbon loss.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Waterlogging Sensitivity & Hypoxia Timeline
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat roots require soil oxygen for aerobic respiration; in waterlogged/saturated soil, oxygen depletion occurs within 24-48 hours. Exposure of 1 to 3 days is generally tolerated with temporary growth pauses if foliage is cool and unflooded; exposure of 3 to 7 days causes seminal root death, reduced tillering, and lower leaf chlorosis (due to impaired N uptake); waterlogging exceeding 7 to 14 days causes severe root necrosis,stand thinning, and 20% to 50% yield reduction depending on stage.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Department of Agriculture Western Australia / University of Western Australia
evidence_registry.source_title: Review of prospects for germplasm improvement for waterlogging tolerance in wheat, barley and oats
evidence_registry.citation_location: Annals of Botany 91(2):145-162, Section: Plant Responses to Waterlogging, pp. 146-150
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Waterlogging displaces soil pore air and dissolved O2 is rapidly depleted by root and microbial respiration within 24 to 48 h... Waterlogging for 7-14 days during vegetative or stem elongation stages reduces grain yield by 20-50%... Seminal roots senesce, and adventitious roots with aerenchyma form near the soil surface.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Comprehensive review of experimental waterlogging data across cereal crops.
evidence_registry.limitations: Waterlogging injury is heavily compounded by warm temperatures; cool winter waterlogging is tolerated longer than warm spring waterlogging.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Salinity Tolerance (ECe Threshold & Slope)
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat is classified as moderately tolerant to soil salinity. The baseline Maas-Hoffman electrical conductivity threshold (ECe) is 6.0 dS/m, with a yield reduction slope of 7.1% per dS/m increase above 6.0 dS/m (Yr = 100 - 7.1*(ECe - 6.0)). Semi-dwarf cultivars (Francois et al., 1986) demonstrate higher salt tolerance with a threshold of 8.6 dS/m and slope of 3.0% per dS/m. Wheat is significantly more salinity-tolerant than corn (threshold 1.7 dS/m) or soybean (threshold 5.0 dS/m).
evidence_registry.source_organization: USDA Agricultural Research Service, U.S. Salinity Laboratory, Riverside, CA
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop salt tolerance-current assessment
evidence_registry.citation_location: ASCE J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103(IR2):115-134, Table 1, p. 119
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Table 1 (Agricultural Crops Salt Tolerance): Wheat (Triticum aestivum): Threshold ECe = 6.0 dS/m; Slope = 7.1% per dS/m; Evaluation: Moderately tolerant.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Root zone saturated paste electrical conductivity (ECe) under standard irrigation management.
evidence_registry.limitations: Seedling emergence stage is more sensitive to salinity than vegetative or ripening stages.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Take-All Root Rot & Monoculture Penalties
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Take-all (Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici / G. tritici) is the primary root and crown disease in continuous wheat systems. A 1- to 2-year non-cereal broadleaf break crop (soybean, canola, field peas, sunflower) starves the soil-borne fungal inoculum, resulting in substantial yield benefits (15-30% yield boost over continuous wheat). Under continuous wheat monoculture, take-all peaks in years 2-4, followed by spontaneous biological suppression ('take-all decline' driven by 2,4-DAPG-producing fluorescent Pseudomonas spp.), though baseline yield remains below break-crop rotations.
evidence_registry.source_organization: USDA Agricultural Research Service / American Phytopathological Society (APS Press)
evidence_registry.source_title: Wheat Health Management
evidence_registry.citation_location: APS Press Monograph, Chapter 4 (Roots and Soilborne Pathogens), pp. 53-72
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Take-all is favored by continuous wheat or barley cropping... Rotating out of cereals for even one season reduces Ggt survival significantly... In monoculture, take-all decline occurs after several years of severe disease due to microbiological antagonism.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. National Wheat Systems (especially PNW, Midwest, and Northern Plains)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: All wheat classes (no commercial cultivars possess complete genetic immunity)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Root infection occurs in moist, cool soils; severe whitehead symptoms manifest under moisture stress during grain fill.
evidence_registry.limitations: Barley, triticale, and grassy weeds (e.g. bromes) serve as alternative hosts and maintain inoculum.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Fusarium Head Blight Carryover from Corn
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Fusarium head blight (FHB / scab) in wheat is caused by Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae), which also causes Gibberella stalk and ear rot in corn. Planting wheat directly into corn residue dramatically elevates FHB spore pressure during wheat flowering, leading to severe yield loss, tombstone kernels, and deoxynivalenol (DON / vomitoxin) contamination (>2.0 ppm triggers elevator dockage or rejection). Soybean is the preferred preceding crop for wheat, lowering localized inoculum and reducing FHB epidemic risk.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Purdue University Extension / The Ohio State University Extension / Crop Protection Network
evidence_registry.source_title: Fusarium Head Blight (Head Scab)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Wise, K., Woloshun, C., Freije, A., Paul, P.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Purdue Extension BP-33-W / CPN-1002, Disease Cycle & Management, pp. 1-4
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Fusarium graminearum survives in corn residue and small grain straw... Planting wheat after corn significantly increases the risk of head scab because corn residue provides abundant inoculum... Rotating to non-host crops like soybean greatly reduces inoculum.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Midwest, Eastern Corn Belt, Northern Plains, and Mid-Atlantic
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Soft Red Winter, Hard Red Spring, and Hard Red Winter wheat
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Disease outbreaks require warm, humid/rainy weather during flowering (Feekes 10.51).
evidence_registry.limitations: Soybean is a minor host for F. graminearum (causing damping-off/pod blight), but does not generate the massive ascospore loads that corn stalks produce.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus & Volunteer Green Bridge
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is transmitted exclusively by the wheat curl mite (Aceria tosichella). The mite and virus require a continuous 'green bridge' of living host tissue to survive between summer wheat harvest and fall wheat emergence. Volunteer wheat is the primary summer reservoir. To break the disease cycle, all volunteer wheat and grassy weeds must be completely terminated via herbicides or tillage at least 2 weeks (ideally 30+ days) prior to planting fall winter wheat so mites starve and desiccate.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Wheat Streak Mosaic
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: De Wolf, E., Andersen Onofre, K., Michaud, J.P.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Publication EP167, Disease Cycle & Control Measures, pp. 1-4
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: The wheat curl mite lives on living green tissue... Volunteer wheat emerging before or during harvest serves as a green bridge... Volunteer wheat must be completely dead for at least two weeks before the new crop emerges to prevent mite migration.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Great Plains (Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Colorado, Montana, South Dakota, Texas)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Winter wheat in Great Plains dryland cropping systems
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Mites are wingless and wind-blown; regional community-wide volunteer control is necessary for field protection.
evidence_registry.limitations: Corn and some summer annual grasses (e.g. foxtails) can host curl mites, though volunteer wheat is by far the primary epidemiological vector.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Dual-Purpose Grazing & First Hollow Stem Stage
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: In the Southern Great Plains (OK, TX, KS), dual-purpose winter wheat is planted early (late Aug - early Sept) for cattle grazing from November through early spring, followed by grain harvest. The physiological cutoff for cattle removal is First Hollow Stem (FHS), defined as 1.5 cm (5/8 inch, diameter of a dime) of hollow stem developing below the embryonic head. Grazing past FHS damages the developing spike and reduces subsequent grain yield by 1% to 5% per day.
evidence_registry.source_title: First Hollow Stem: A Critical Wheat Growth Stage for Dual-Purpose Producers
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: de Oliveira Silva, A., Edwards, J.T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: First hollow stem occurs when there is 1.5 cm (5/8 in) of hollow stem below the developing wheat head... Grazing past first hollow stem reduces grain yield by 1 to 5 percent per day... Cattle must be removed to avoid crushing the growing point.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Southern Great Plains (Oklahoma, Texas Panhandle, Southern Kansas)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Hard red winter wheat dual-purpose cultivars
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Early-seeded wheat with adequate fall moisture and stocking rates (typically 1-2 acres per stocker steer).
evidence_registry.limitations: Earlier planting for forage increases susceptibility to fall armyworm, Hessian fly, and wheat streak mosaic virus.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Double-Cropping Winter Wheat & Soybean
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Double-cropping winter wheat followed immediately by soybean is widely viable south of approximately 39°N to 40°N latitude (Kentucky, southern Illinois/Indiana, Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee, Virginia, Kansas). Primary limiting factors are late-season moisture depletion by maturing wheat and shortened soybean photoperiod. Delaying double-crop soybean planting past late June / early July imposes a yield penalty of 0.5 to 1.0 bushel/acre per day of delay. Harvesting wheat at 18-20% grain moisture and artificial drying accelerates soybean seeding by 3-5 days.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Service
evidence_registry.source_title: Double-Cropping Wheat and Soybeans
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Lee, C., Herbek, J., Mansfield, K.
evidence_registry.citation_location: University of Kentucky Bulletin ID-185, Chapters 1-3, pp. 5-14
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Double-cropping soybeans after wheat provides two cash crops in one year... Soybean yield potential decreases by roughly 0.5 to 1.0 bu/acre per day delayed past late June... Soil moisture at planting is the primary determinant of emergence.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Mid-South, Ohio Valley, Southern Corn Belt (latitudes < 39-40°N)
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Early-maturing Soft Red Winter wheat and Maturity Group 3-5 Soybeans
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Requires no-till drilling of soybeans directly into wheat stubble to conserve moisture.
evidence_registry.limitations: In drought years, double-crop soybean stands fail to emerge or suffer severe summer abortion.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Soil Acidity & Aluminum Toxicity Threshold
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat grows optimally between soil pH 6.0 and 7.5. When soil pH drops below 5.5, insoluble aluminum-containing minerals dissolve into toxic trivalent aluminum (Al3+). Free Al3+ inhibits cell division in wheat root tips, causing short, stubby, brown, club-shaped roots, severe stunting, and impaired P uptake. Liming is triggered when soil pH falls below 5.5 to neutralize Al3+ and restore root elongation. Certain varieties carry ALMT1 (aluminum-activated malate transporter) genes conferring moderate low-pH tolerance.
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Acid Soils for Wheat Production
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Zhang, H., Raun, W., Edwards, J.T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: At soil pH below 5.5, aluminum becomes soluble and toxic to wheat root systems... Toxic Al3+ burns root tips, resulting in stunted, club-shaped roots... Yield is severely reduced unless lime is applied or Al-tolerant varieties are planted.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Southern Great Plains, Eastern Washington Palouse, and Southeast
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Acidification accelerated by long-term ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizer applications.
evidence_registry.limitations: Surface-applied lime without tillage in no-till fields takes several years to neutralize subsoil acidity.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Herbicide Rotational Restrictions & pH Dependency
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rotational plant-back intervals for wheat and rotational crops following wheat are strictly product-label specific: Fomesafen (Flexstar, EPA Reg. No. 100-1101) mandates a 4.5-month plant-back interval for small grains (wheat). Atrazine (AAtrex 4L, EPA Reg. No. 100-497) restricts fall-seeded small grains following corn/sorghum application. In wheat, sulfonylurea herbicides like chlorsulfuron (Finesse/Glean) degrade via chemical hydrolysis, which is severely retarded in high pH soils (pH > 7.0 to 7.9). In alkaline soils, chlorsulfuron persistence can exceed 24 to 36 months, prohibiting rotation to sensitive broadleaves (sunflower, sorghum, non-STS soybean).
evidence_registry.source_organization: U.S. EPA / K-State Research and Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: EPA Pesticide Product Labels & Extension Weed Management Guides
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency / Syngenta / Corteva / K-State Extension
evidence_registry.citation_location: EPA Reg. Nos. 100-1101, 100-497, 352-522, 279-3610; KSU Chem. Weed Control MF258
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Flexstar label: 4.5 month plant-back to small grains. Glean/Finesse label: Do not use on soils with pH greater than 7.9; rotational intervals to sensitive crops extend to 24-36 months in alkaline soils due to inhibited chemical hydrolysis.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Herbicide formulations applied in corn, soy, and wheat rotations
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Federal FIFRA pesticide registration legal mandates; actual breakdown dependent on rainfall and pH.
evidence_registry.limitations: Product formulations, tank mixes, and regional supplemental labels establish exact legal intervals.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Staging & Management Windows
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Spring wheat development progresses continuously across 85-115 days without winter dormancy: Germination/Emergence (Zadoks 00-10, 7-14 days), Tillering (Zadoks 20-29, 2-4 weeks), Stem Elongation / Jointing (Zadoks 30-39, 2-3 weeks; critical for final weed control and jointing-stage growth regulator application), Booting and Heading (Zadoks 40-59, 1-2 weeks), Anthesis (Zadoks 60-69, 3-5 days; critical window for triazole fungicide application to manage Fusarium head blight), and Milk/Dough Ripening (Zadoks 70-92, 4-5 weeks to physiological maturity indicated by complete loss of green color from peduncle).
evidence_registry.source_title: Growth and Development Guide for Spring Wheat
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Simmons, S.R., Oelke, E.A., Anderson, P.M.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Extension Folder AG-FO-2547, Zadoks & Feekes Scale Descriptions, pp. 1-12
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: The guide outlines the Zadoks decimal code from 0 to 9 for spring wheat... Herbicide applications must cease before jointing (Zadoks 30/Feekes 6)... Fungicides for scab must be timed at early flowering (Zadoks 60-65).
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Northern Plains and Upper Midwest
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard staging framework for agronomic decision support in spring small grains.
evidence_registry.limitations: Development rate accelerates substantially if mean daily temperatures exceed 22-25°C in June/July.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Residue Cover, Water Conservation, & Soil Carbon
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Standing wheat stubble traps winter snow, reduces wind speed at the soil surface by 50-70%, and suppresses soil evaporation during subsequent fallow or early growth of following crops. In Great Plains ecofallow/no-till systems, maintaining wheat residue increases soil water storage efficiency by 15-25% over conventional tillage. While surface residue decomposes slowly due to high C:N, long-term soil organic carbon (SOC) accrual is heavily driven by below-ground fine root turnover rather than straw alone, with humification efficiency of straw carbon typically limited to 8-15%.
evidence_registry.source_title: Tillage, nitrogen, and cropping system effects on soil carbon sequestration
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Halvorson, A.D., Wienhold, B.J., Black, A.L.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Soil Science Society of America Journal / Agronomy Journal 94(3):442-449, pp. 445-448
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Annual cropping with wheat under no-till increased SOC compared to crop-fallow... High residue production protects soil from erosion, but root-derived carbon contributes proportionately more to stable SOC pools than surface straw.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: U.S. Great Plains and Pacific Northwest Dryland Systems
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Winter and spring wheat dryland cropping systems
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Long-term (12+ year) dryland tillage and rotation experiment in Northern Great Plains.
evidence_registry.limitations: SOC sequestration rates vary with baseline soil texture, initial carbon content, and precipitation.

evidence_registry.source_title: Chemical Weed Control for Field Crops, Pastures, and Noncropland, Report of Progress SRP-1169
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Atrazine safener (fluxofenim / Concep III) is mandatory for using chloroacetamide herbicides (S-metolachlor) on sorghum.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Un-safened seed suffers severe chlorosis and stand loss from metolachlor.
evidence_registry.limitations: Plant-back restrictions to small grains or legumes must be observed.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Wheat-Sorghum-Fallow (W-S-F) Dryland System Synergy
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat-Sorghum-Fallow produces two cash crops in three years, conserving moisture in standing wheat stubble for no-till sorghum emergence.
evidence_registry.source_organization: USDA-ARS Conservation and Production Research Laboratory
evidence_registry.source_title: Dryland Agriculture, Agronomy Monograph No. 23 & Peterson et al. (1996)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Peterson, G.A. et al. / Unger, P.W.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Agron. Monogr. 23 pp. 385–418; J. Prod. Agric. 9:180–186
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Standing wheat stubble traps winter snow and reduces soil evaporation, providing 50-75 mm extra water for sorghum.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Hard red winter wheat and grain sorghum
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: No-till or ecofallow chemical weed control.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires adequate weed management during summer fallow to prevent moisture depletion.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Grain Sorghum
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Kansas: Plant May 15 – June 20, Harvest Sept 25 – Nov 10; Texas: Plant March 1 – May 15 (South) / May 15 – June 25 (Plains), Harvest July 1 – Aug 15 (South) / Oct 1 – Nov 20 (Plains).
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Primary state planting and harvesting windows based on historical field records.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Statewide 80% active distribution windows.
evidence_registry.limitations: Weather anomalies and soil temperatures (<15°C) alter field entry dates.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Deficit Irrigation Response & Heat Adaptation in High Plains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Sorghum maintains 80–90% yield potential under 50% deficit irrigation (150–250 mm net), outperforming corn under restricted water allocations.
evidence_registry.source_title: Grain Sorghum Irrigation Management in the Texas High Plains, Bul. B-6048
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Targeted irrigation at boot and grain fill maximizes water productivity when full irrigation is economically infeasible.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Pumping capacities restricted by declining Ogallala Aquifer levels.
evidence_registry.limitations: Severe drought during panicle initiation permanently limits seed number per head.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Taxonomy, Growth Habit & USDA Symbol
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Gossypium hirsutum L. (Symbol: GOHI), Malvaceae, indeterminate woody perennial grown as annual row crop.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Upland cotton; accounts for >95% of U.S. cotton production.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Encompasses standard commercial picker and stripper varieties.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excludes Pima / Extra Long Staple (Gossypium barbadense L.).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Phenology, DD60 Heat Units & Indeterminate Growth Habit
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: 130–180 active growth days; DD60 base temp 15.6°C (60°F); 2,100–2,600 DD60-F (1,167–1,444 DD-C) to boll opening; indeterminate flowering.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Georgia Extension / Mississippi State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Cotton Production Guide (UGA Bull 501) & Ritchie et al. (2007) Cotton Growth & Development
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Ritchie, G.L., Bednarz, C.W., Jost, P.H., and Brown, S.M.
evidence_registry.citation_location: UGA Bull 501 pp. 4–12; Ritchie et al. pp. 1–28
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: DD60 = [(T_max + T_min)/2] - 60°F; first square at 400-500 DD60, first flower at 750-850 DD60, open boll at 1800-2200 DD60.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Indeterminate habit managed with mepiquat chloride plant growth regulators (PGR).
evidence_registry.limitations: Defoliation and chemical boll opening required for mechanical harvesting.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Thermal Thresholds, Reproductive Heat Stress & Empirical Breakpoints
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: T_base 15.6°C, optimum 25–32°C day / 20–24°C night, square/boll shed >32–35°C day or >24°C night, empirical breakpoint 32.0°C.
evidence_registry.source_title: Physiological responses of cotton to high temperature (Snider et al. 2009) & Schlenker & Roberts (2009)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Snider, J.L. et al. / Schlenker, W. and Roberts, M.J.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Night temperatures >24°C deplete carbohydrate reserves via dark respiration; temperatures >35°C inhibit pollen tube elongation, causing abscission.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Evaluated during peak bloom (July-August).
evidence_registry.limitations: High humidity exacerbates night respiration stress in Delta and Southeast.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Consumptive Water Use (ETc), Drought & Waterlogging Response
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 600–900 mm (24–36 in); peak 7–10 mm/d at peak bloom; moderate drought tolerance via taproot; highly sensitive to soil anoxia/waterlogging.
evidence_registry.source_title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 & Cotton Water Management (B-6048)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. (FAO) / Bordovsky, J. et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cotton sheds fruit during water stress to prioritize survival; soil waterlogging >24-48 h causes ethylene synthesis, resulting in severe square shedding.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Rainfed in Southeast; furrow/drip irrigated in Southwest and High Plains.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excessive late-season water delays boll opening and promotes rank vegetative growth.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Soil pH, Acidity, Salinity Threshold & Aluminum Sensitivity
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 6.0–7.0; tolerated 5.5–8.2; Salinity threshold ECe 7.7 dS/m (tolerant), slope 5.2% per dS/m; highly sensitive to aluminum at pH <5.5.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977) & Cotton Fertility Guide
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Mitchell, C.C. and Phillips, S.
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103:115–134; Auburn Ext. ANR-0252
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cotton is one of the most salt-tolerant row crops; however, seedling taproots are severely pruned by subsoil aluminum toxicity at pH <5.5.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard saturated extract ECe.
evidence_registry.limitations: Seedling emergence is moderately sensitive to salinity (ECe >4.0 dS/m), even though mature plants are tolerant.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Root Architecture, Effective Extraction & Compaction Sensitivity
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 90–120 cm (3.0–4.0 ft); maximum taproot penetration 150–200 cm (5.0–6.5 ft); prominent taproot; highly sensitive to hardpans.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & The role of root system in water uptake (Agron. J.)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: USDA-NRCS / Taylor, H.M. and Klepper, B.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vigorous central taproot with lateral branches; impenetrable traffic pans at 15-25 cm cause J-rooting and shallow drought stress (paradoxtilling/subsoiling needed).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep sandy loam or alluvial soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Plow pans without subsoiling restrict effective depth to <30-45 cm.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Nutrient Removal Per Bale & Total Seasonal Uptake
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Removal per 480 lb lint bale (+seed): 35 lb N (15.9 kg N), 14 lb P2O5 (6.4 kg P2O5), 20 lb K2O (9.1 kg K2O); Total uptake per bale: 50–60 lb N, 20–25 lb P2O5, 50–60 lb K2O.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Potash & Phosphate Institute (PPI) / Mississippi State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Nutrient Deficiencies and Accretion in Cotton, Pub. 2404
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Oldham, L. / International Plant Nutrition Institute (IPNI)
evidence_registry.citation_location: MSU Ext. Pub. 2404 pp. 1–6; IPNI Nutri-Facts No. 4
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Seed cotton accounts for primary N and P export; burrs and leaves retain significant K, but K must be immediately available during peak boll fill (2-4 lb K2O/ac/day).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: 480 lb lint bale yielding ~700 lb cottonseed.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excessive N fertility stimulates vegetative rank growth, delays maturity, and increases boll rot.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Residue Dynamics, C:N Ratio, Erosion Vulnerability & Net N Balance
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 4,500–7,500 kg/ha; C:N ratio 40:1–60:1; residue N 1.0–1.5%; residue N content 40–75 kg N/ha; net soil N balance -120 to -60 kg N/ha; credit 0 lb N/ac; low soil cover.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cotton Residue Management and Soil Organic Matter Dynamics in the Southeast
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Raper, R.L., Reeves, D.W., and Burmester, C.H.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cotton residue is woody and brittle, providing sparse surface ground cover (<30% cover post-harvest), leaving soils prone to winter wind and water erosion.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Winter cover crops (rye, clover) strongly recommended to provide soil protection.
evidence_registry.limitations: Does not provide fertilizer N credit to succeeding crops.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Continuous Cotton Monoculture Penalty & Soilborne Disease Buildup
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Continuous cotton causes 10–20% yield decline; escalates Verticillium wilt (Verticillium dahliae), reniform nematode (Rotylenchulus reniformis), and root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension / Cotton Incorporated
evidence_registry.source_title: Cotton Disease Management and Nematode Control, Research Compendium
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Continuous monoculture without resistant varieties leads to severe nematode reproduction and compounding vascular wilt disease complexes.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field infestation with nematodes or Verticillium microsclerotia.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires fumigants or nematicides and resistant cultivars if rotated infrequently.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cotton-Corn Rotational Synergy & Nematode Suppression
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Corn is a non-host to reniform nematode (Rotylenchulus reniformis); rotating cotton with corn suppresses reniform populations and increases subsequent cotton yields by 10–18%.
evidence_registry.source_title: Reniform Nematode Management in Mississippi Cotton, Pub. 2426
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rotating out of cotton to corn for a single season reduces reniform nematode numbers below economic damage thresholds.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Moderate to severe initial reniform nematode pressure.
evidence_registry.limitations: Corn and cotton share susceptibility to root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita); monitor nematode species identity.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Herbicide Sensitivities & Carryover Restrictions in Cotton
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Cotton is sensitive to ALS inhibitors, atrazine (12-18 month plant-back), and off-target 2,4-D or dicamba auxin drift on non-tolerant trait varieties.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Recommended Weed Control for Arkansas Field Crops, MP44
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Conventional and non-auxin tolerant cotton varieties suffer catastrophic epinasty and square abortion from sub-lethal auxin drift.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Trait matching (Enlist vs XtendFlex) strictly required.
evidence_registry.limitations: Ensure rotational herbicide plant-backs are strictly verified.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cotton-Sorghum Rotational Compatibility in High Plains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rotating cotton with grain sorghum breaks cotton root-knot nematode and Verticillium wilt; sorghum residue protects light sandy soils from wind erosion.
evidence_registry.source_title: Long-term Cotton and Grain Sorghum Cropping Systems in the Rolling Plains of Texas
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: DeLaune, P.B., Sij, J.W., Park, S.C., and Krutz, L.J.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Sorghum rotation increases cotton lint yield by 12-15% and provides critical residue cover to shield tender emerging cotton seedlings from blowing sand.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Texas Rolling Plains & Southern High Plains
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Semiarid dryland and deficit irrigated production.
evidence_registry.limitations: Manage sorghum residue N tie-up in early spring.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Cotton
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Texas: Plant April 15 – June 20, Harvest Sept 15 – Dec 15; Mississippi/Delta: Plant April 25 – May 25, Harvest Sept 20 – Nov 10; Georgia/Southeast: Plant April 20 – May 31, Harvest Oct 1 – Dec 1.
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Statewide usual active planting and harvesting progress distributions across Cotton Belt.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Minimum soil temperature 18°C (65°F) at 8:00 AM for 3 consecutive days prior to planting.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cold wet soils at planting induce severe seedling disease (Pythium, Rhizoctonia) and stand failure.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Deficit Drip Irrigation & Water Productivity in Texas High Plains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Subsurface drip irrigation (SDI) delivers 250–500 mm net irrigation, boosting water use efficiency to 0.4–0.8 kg lint/m³ and minimizing evaporative losses.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cotton Yield and Water Use Efficiency under Subsurface Drip Irrigation (Bordovsky & Mustian 2004)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: SDI applied at 75% of full crop ETc achieved lint yields comparable to 100% ETc, preserving groundwater.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deficit irrigation managed to avoid excessive vegetative growth.
evidence_registry.limitations: High capital setup cost; rodent damage to drip tape during winter.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Taxonomy, Subspecies, Growth Habit & USDA Symbol
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Oryza sativa L. (Symbol: ORSA), Poaceae, semi-aquatic C3 annual grass; Southern long-grain (indica) and California medium-grain (japonica).
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oryza sativa L.; adapted to flooded anaerobic conditions via continuous lysigenous aerenchyma tissue.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Commercial lowland paddy rice.
evidence_registry.limitations: Strictly lowland/flooded rice; excludes upland wild rice (Zizania palustris L.).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Phenology, DD50 Thermal Units & Water Seeding / Drill Seeding Systems
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: 105–140 active growth days; DD50 base temp 10.0°C (50°F); 2,100–2,800 DD50-F (1,167–1,556 GDD-C) to harvest maturity; drill-seeded delayed flood and water-seeded systems.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Arkansas Rice Production Handbook, Extension Bulletin MP192
evidence_registry.citation_location: UADA MP192 'Rice Growth and Development' pp. 11–24
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: DD50 program predicts panicle differentiation, heading, and drain dates based on cumulative heat units.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Flood established at 4-5 leaf stage (drill-seeded).
evidence_registry.limitations: Late-planted rice exposed to fall cool snaps during flowering causes high blanking.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Thermal Thresholds, Cold Blanking & Heat-Induced Chalkiness
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: T_base 10.0°C, optimum 25–33°C, cold blanking threshold <15.0°C at microsporogenesis, heat stress >35°C (night >24°C impairs milling quality and head rice yield).
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of California Davis / International Rice Research Institute
evidence_registry.source_title: Rice Production Manual (UC Davis Pub 21623) & Board, J.E. (Cold Blanking in California Rice)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Linquist, B.A., Mutters, R.G., and Greer, C.A.
evidence_registry.citation_location: UC Davis Pub 21623 pp. 15–28; Agron. J. 72:483–487
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Night temperatures <15°C during pollen development cause microspore abortion (blanking); deep flood water (15-20 cm) acts as thermal blanket.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Water depth managed dynamically for cold protection.
evidence_registry.limitations: Mid-South long grains highly sensitive to nighttime heat stress during grain filling (>24°C).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Consumptive Water Use (ETc), Flood Irrigation Dynamics & Anoxia Adaptation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 700–900 mm (28–35 in); total water input 750–1,500 mm (30–60 in); 100% irrigated; highly flood-tolerant via aerenchyma; extremely sensitive to drought.
evidence_registry.source_title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 & Henry et al. (2016) Water Management in Rice
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. (FAO) / Henry, C.G.
evidence_registry.citation_location: FAO 33 Section 'Rice' pp. 125–130; UADA MP192 pp. 75–94
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Continuous flood (5-10 cm) controls weeds and optimizes nutrient availability; moisture stress below saturation during panicle initiation causes catastrophic yield loss.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Precision land leveling and zero-grade / contour levee management.
evidence_registry.limitations: Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) saves water but requires strict monitoring to prevent yield decline.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Soil pH, Anaerobic Soil Chemistry, Impermeable Hardpan & Salinity Threshold
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 5.5–6.8 (neutralizes toward 6.5–7.0 under submergence); tolerated 4.8–7.8; Salinity threshold ECe 3.0 dS/m (moderately sensitive), slope 12.0% per dS/m; requires impermeable hardpan.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977) & Slaton et al. (Rice Soil Fertility)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Slaton, N.A. et al.
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103:115–134; UADA MP192 pp. 45–62
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Anaerobic flooding reduces ferric iron to ferrous and increases pH of acid soils; saline irrigation water (>2.0 dS/m) severely stunts seedlings.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Soils with high clay content (Sharkey clay, Crowley silt loam) to minimize percolation.
evidence_registry.limitations: Alkaline or calcareous soils (pH >7.5) cause severe zinc deficiency (seedling chlorosis) upon flooding.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Root Architecture, Effective Extraction Depth & Aerenchyma Tissue
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 30–60 cm (1.0–2.0 ft); maximum anatomical penetration 60–90 cm (2.0–3.0 ft); superficial adventitious root mat with continuous aerenchyma.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Yoshida (1981) Fundamentals of Rice Crop Science
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: >90% of rice roots reside in top 20 cm of reduced soil; internal gas channels transport atmospheric oxygen from shoot to root tips.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Flooded paddy with restrictive plow pan at 15-25 cm.
evidence_registry.limitations: Restricted root volume makes plants extremely vulnerable if flood is lost.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Nutrient Removal, Anaerobic Nitrogen Dynamics & Urea Management
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Removal per 45 lb bushel: 0.60 lb N (13.3 kg N/t), 0.30 lb P2O5 (6.7 kg P2O5/t), 0.18 lb K2O (4.0 kg K2O/t); requires ammonium-forming N (urea); nitrate denitrifies rapidly.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Rice Soil Fertility and Fertilizer Recommendations, MP192 Chapter 7
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Slaton, N.A., Roberts, T.L., and Hardke, J.T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Pre-flood urea must be applied onto dry soil and flooded within 2-3 days to incorporate N into reduced zone, preventing volatile ammonia loss and denitrification.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard 150-180 bu/ac yield target.
evidence_registry.limitations: Nitrate forms of nitrogen cannot be used under flooded conditions due to total denitrification.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Biomass Production, High Silica Residue, C:N Ratio & Net N Balance
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 7,000–11,000 kg/ha; C:N ratio 50:1–70:1; residue N 0.6–0.9%; residue N content 45–75 kg N/ha; net soil N balance -130 to -80 kg N/ha; credit 0 lb N/ac; high silica (10–15%).
evidence_registry.source_title: Rice Straw Management and Decomposition in Temperate Lowlands (Linquist et al. 2006)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Linquist, B.A. et al. / Bird, J.A. and Horwath, W.R.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: High silica content and lignin retard decomposition; winter flooding promotes anaerobic breakdown and provides winter waterfowl habitat.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Straw chopped and rolled or incorporated post-harvest.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excessive straw under cold water generates organic acids and hydrogen sulfide toxic to seedling roots.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Continuous Rice Monoculture Penalty, Sheath Blight & Red Rice
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Continuous rice causes 10–25% yield loss; drives rapid buildup of sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani), weedy red rice (Oryza sativa f. spontanea), and straighthead disorder.
evidence_registry.source_title: Rice Disease Management (MP192 Chapter 11) & Louisiana Rice Production Handbook
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Hardke, J.T., Cartwright, R.D., and Groth, D.E.
evidence_registry.citation_location: UADA MP192 pp. 115–136; LSU AgCenter Pub. 2321
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rhizoctonia sclerotia float on flood water and accumulate across seasons; red rice cannot be selectively controlled in conventional rice.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Unrotated paddy fields.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires rotating to soybean or using Clearfield/FullPage/Provisia herbicide-tolerant systems.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Rice-Soybean Rotational Synergy in the Mid-South
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rice-Soybean rotation (1:1 or 2:1) is the premier Mid-South system; allows selective grass/red rice control with ALS/ACCase herbicides and improves soil drainage.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Economic and Agronomic Benefits of Rice-Soybean Crop Rotations, Research Series 581
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Soybean breaks the sheath blight fungal cycle, utilizes residual phosphorus, and allows intensive weed control programs against red rice.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Commercial long-grain rice and Maturity Group IV/V soybean
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Adequate surface drainage to prevent waterlogging during soybean phase.
evidence_registry.limitations: Soybean yields on heavy clay rice soils depend critically on timely furrow irrigation.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Herbicide Sensitivities & Carryover Restrictions in Rice
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rice is sensitive to atrazine (18-month plant-back under flood), fomesafen, and ALS carryover; Clearfield (imidazolinone) rice carries strict plant-back rules.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Recommended Weed Control for Arkansas Field Crops, MP44
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Norsworthy, J.K., Barber, L.T., and Hardke, J.T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Atrazine residue in flooded anaerobic soil causes catastrophic chlorosis and stand death; observe label plant-backs.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: High organic matter and flooded field conditions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Stewardship agreements mandate rotating Clearfield rice to non-Clearfield crops to prevent outcrossing with red rice.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Rice-Wheat Rotational Sequencing in the Delta
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter wheat can be seeded after early rice harvest, but late harvest or rutted waterlogged clay soils impede wheat stand establishment.
evidence_registry.source_title: Rice-Wheat Cropping Systems in the Gulf Coast, Pub. 2844
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Requires early rice harvest (late August/early September) and field drainage to allow tillage and drilling before late autumn rains.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Soft red winter wheat and long-grain rice
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Well-drained silt loam or bedded rice ground.
evidence_registry.limitations: Poorly drained heavy clay soils frequently waterlog wheat seedlings, causing severe stand loss.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Rice
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Arkansas: Plant April 10 – May 25, Harvest Aug 25 – Oct 15; California: Plant April 25 – May 20, Harvest Sept 15 – Nov 1; Louisiana: Plant March 15 – April 30, Harvest July 20 – Sept 15.
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Statewide usual active planting and harvesting progress distributions across Rice production areas.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Drill-seeded in Mid-South; water-seeded into flooded checks in California.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring flood delays or high river stages delay field entry.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Row Rice / Furrow-Irrigated Rice (FIR) System Adaptation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Furrow-irrigated rice eliminates continuous levees, reducing water use by 15–30% and facilitating rotation with corn and soybean.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
evidence_registry.source_title: Furrow-Irrigated Rice Handbook, Extension Bulletin MP562
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Henry, C.G., Hardke, J.T., and Chlapecka, Z.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Grown on raised beds using poly-pipe surge irrigation; increases risk of rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae) and N loss via nitrification/denitrification cycles.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Arkansas, Mississippi, and Missouri Bootheel Delta
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fields with 0.1 to 0.3% slope.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires blast-resistant hybrids and split nitrogen management to maintain yield parity with flooded rice.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Taxonomy, Row Types, Growth Habit & USDA Symbol
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Hordeum vulgare L. (Symbol: HOVU), Poaceae, cool-season C3 cereal; 2-row and 6-row types; Spring and Winter growth habits.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hordeum vulgare L. ssp. vulgare; includes malting and feed market classes.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Single canonical entity encompassing spring and winter growth types.
evidence_registry.limitations: Strictly domesticated barley; excludes wild barley (Hordeum spontaneum).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Phenology, GDD Base Temperature & Vernalization Habits
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth: Spring 70–95 d, Winter 115–150 d; Calendar: Spring 85–110 d, Winter 210–270 d; GDD base 0.0°C; Vernalization: Spring 0 d, Winter 30–50 d at 0–7°C (Vrn-H1 regulation).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Montana State University Extension / North Dakota State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Barley Growth and Development, EB0161 & NDSU Extension A-540
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Wiersma, J.J. et al. / Franck, S.
evidence_registry.citation_location: MSU EB0161 pp. 1–8; NDSU A-540 pp. 1–12
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Spring barley matures earlier than spring wheat, escaping late-summer heat and drought; winter barley requires cold accumulation for spikelet initiation.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains, Intermountain West, and Mid-Atlantic
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Base 0°C (32°F) standard small-grain calculation.
evidence_registry.limitations: Winter barley is less cold-hardy than winter wheat (-12 to -15°C vs -20°C kill threshold).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Malting Quality Standards & Protein Thresholds
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: AMBA malting specifications: grain protein 11.5–13.5% (>13.5% rejected to feed); plump kernels >80%; germination energy >95%; DON <1.0 ppm.
evidence_registry.source_title: Malting Barley Quality Factors and Evaluation Standards
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: High N fertility or late heat stress spikes grain protein above 13.5%, causing severe price discounting to feed market.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard clean commercial deliveries.
evidence_registry.limitations: Strict rejection thresholds make nitrogen and irrigation management precision-critical.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Thermal Thresholds, Anthesis Heat Sensitivity & Frost Limits
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: T_base 0.0°C, optimum 15–22°C, heat stress >28–30°C (shrivels kernels, spikes protein), empirical breakpoint 29–30°C; frost limit: spring -4 to -6°C, winter -12 to -15°C.
evidence_registry.source_title: Heat stress impacts on grain development in barley & Schlenker & Roberts (2009)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Wallwork, M.A.B. et al. / Schlenker, W. and Roberts, M.J.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Barley is sensitive to high temperature during grain fill; temperatures >30°C truncate starch synthesis.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field grain filling conditions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring barley avoids heat by early heading, but late-planted crops suffer heavy malting rejection.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Consumptive Water Use (ETc), Drought Escapement & Waterlogging Sensitivity
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 350–550 mm (14–22 in); peak 5–7 mm/d at boot/heading; drought tolerant/escaping via short season; highly sensitive to waterlogging (most sensitive of small grains).
evidence_registry.source_title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 & Barley Water Use, EB0161
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. (FAO) / Bauder, J.W.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Barley produces highest grain per unit water among temperate cereals under dry conditions; anaerobic soil conditions for 48 h cause severe chlorosis and tillering failure.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep well-drained soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Unsuitable for poorly drained clay soils or high-water-table positions.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Soil pH, Acidity Sensitivity & Superior Salinity Tolerance
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 6.0–7.5; tolerated 5.5–8.5; Salinity threshold ECe 8.0 dS/m (the most salt-tolerant commercial grain crop), slope 5.0% per dS/m; highly sensitive to aluminum at pH <5.8.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977) & Fertilizer Guidelines for Montana Crops
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Jones, C. and Jacobsen, J.
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103:115–134; MSU EB0161
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Barley is the premier reclamation and saline-seep crop in the Northern Plains; however, it is extraordinarily sensitive to soil acidity and soluble aluminum.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard saturated paste electrical conductivity.
evidence_registry.limitations: Severe yield collapse occurs below pH 5.5 unless limed.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Root Architecture, Effective Extraction Depth & Penetration
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 75–120 cm (2.5–4.0 ft); maximum anatomical penetration 120–180 cm (4.0–6.0 ft); dense fibrous root system.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Weaver (1926) Root Development of Field Crops
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Dense seminal and nodal roots permeate the upper 60-90 cm, with leading tapers reaching 150-180 cm in deep silt loams.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep unconstrained soil profiles.
evidence_registry.limitations: Subsoil acidity or compaction restricts roots to shallow layers.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Grain Nutrient Removal Rates & Malting Nitrogen Management
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Removal per 48 lb bushel: 0.78 lb N (16.2 kg N/t), 0.38 lb P2O5 (7.9 kg P2O5/t), 0.25 lb K2O (5.2 kg K2O/t); Total uptake per bushel: 1.10–1.30 lb N.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Montana State University Extension / North Dakota State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Fertilizer Guidelines for Montana Crops, EB0161 & NDSU SF-723
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Jones, C. and Jacobsen, J. / Franzen, D.
evidence_registry.citation_location: MSU EB0161 pp. 8–14; NDSU SF-723 pp. 1–6
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Malting barley requires precise N budgeting (1.2–1.3 lb available N/bu total supply including soil test nitrate) to avoid exceeding 13.5% protein.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: 48 lb/bushel standard test weight.
evidence_registry.limitations: Feed barley can utilize higher N rates (1.5 lb N/bu) for maximum yield.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Biomass Production, Residue C:N, Decomposition & Net N Balance
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 4,000–7,000 kg/ha; C:N ratio 60:1–80:1; residue N 0.6–0.9%; residue N content 25–50 kg N/ha; net soil N balance -90 to -50 kg N/ha; credit 0 lb N/ac (immobilizes 15–30 lb N/ac).
evidence_registry.source_organization: USDA-ARS Northern Great Plains Research Laboratory
evidence_registry.source_title: Residue Management and Carbon Sequestration in Northern Great Plains Cropping Systems
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Halvorson, A.D., Wienhold, B.J., and Black, A.L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Barley straw decomposes slowly; high C:N ratio immobilizes early spring soil nitrogen, mitigating nitrate leaching during winter in winter barley systems.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Residue retained on surface in no-till or conservation tillage.
evidence_registry.limitations: Starter N required on subsequent crops planted into heavy barley stubble.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Continuous Barley Monoculture Penalty, Scald & Net Blotch
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Continuous barley monoculture causes 15–30% yield loss; escalates stubble-borne net blotch (Pyrenophora teres), scald (Rhynchosporium secalis), and spot blotch (Cochliobolus sativus).
evidence_registry.source_title: Barley Disease Management, Extension Bulletin PP-803
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Foliar blotch pathogens survive in infected barley stubble; continuous cropping creates massive early-season inoculum, defoliating flag leaves.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Conservation tillage with surface residue.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires multi-mode foliar fungicides and resistant varieties if rotated continuously.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Corn-Barley Rotation & Fusarium Head Blight (Scab) Risk
