evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Planting barley following corn carries severe Fusarium Head Blight (Fusarium graminearum) risk; DON contamination >1.0 ppm causes total malting rejection.
evidence_registry.source_organization: American Malting Barley Association / NDSU Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Scab in Malting Barley, AMBA Technical Note
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Corn residue is the primary overwintering substrate for Gibberella zeae perithecia; planting malting barley directly into corn stubble is strongly cautioned.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: High humidity or rain during heading/flowering.
evidence_registry.limitations: Strict caution: require scab-tolerant varieties and triazole fungicide at heading.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Winter Barley-Double Crop Soybean Rotation Synergy
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter barley matures 1–2 weeks earlier than winter wheat, enabling double-crop soybean planting by early to mid-June with 100% full-season yield potential in Mid-Atlantic/Upper South.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Virginia Cooperative Extension / Penn State Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Winter Barley as a Double-Crop Option, Pub. 424-035
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Thomason, W.E., Beahm, B.R., and Alley, M.M.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Harvesting winter barley in early June provides a 10-14 day head start over wheat for double-crop soybean emergence, capturing higher summer photoperiod.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Mid-Atlantic, Ohio Valley, and Upper South
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Drilled immediately into harvested barley stubble.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires timely autumn barley seeding (late September to mid-October) to ensure winter survival.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Barley
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Spring Barley (ND, MT, ID): Plant April 15 – May 20, Harvest July 25 – Sept 10; Winter Barley (VA, PA, NC): Plant Sept 25 – Oct 30, Harvest June 5 – June 25.
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Statewide active progress percentiles for spring and winter barley.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: 80% active field operation windows.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring planting delays severely impact malting quality.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Barley-Wheat Sequential Cereal Rotational Risks
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Sequential small-grain rotations (Barley after Wheat or Wheat after Barley) share take-all root rot, Cephalosporium stripe, and risk volunteer contamination.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cereal Rotations in the Pacific Northwest, PNW Bul. 560
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Volunteer barley in wheat downgrades milling grade; shared crown and foot rot pathogens build up in cereal-after-cereal monocultures.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Consecutive small-grain cropping.
evidence_registry.limitations: Include broadleaf crops (canola, pulse, soybean) as intervening break crops.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Growth Duration & Portfolio Role of Cereal Rye
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Secale cereale L., Poaceae, diploid (2n=14), cool-season annual grass; 180-240 days cover crop, 240-280 days full grain.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database: Secale cereale L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Secale cereale L., cereal rye, cool-season annual grass; standard overwintering cover crop and commercial grain.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard agronomic taxonomy.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring rye cultivars exist but comprise <2% of North American acreage.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Fall Seeding, Vernalization & Spring Termination Windows
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 0.0-4.4°C; obligate vernalization (30-60 d at 0-7°C); cumulative GDD to boot 900-1200, to grain 1800-2200.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Midwest Cover Crops Council
evidence_registry.source_title: Cereal Rye Cover Crop Management for Corn and Soybean, AY-356-W
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Johnson, K., Camberato, J., and Legleiter, T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Winter rye requires cold vernalization to head; germination begins at 34°F (1°C); terminates in April-May before cash crops.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Drilled or broadcast seeded in autumn.
evidence_registry.limitations: Late spring termination after heading significantly increases stover C:N ratio and N tie-up.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Peak Water Extraction
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: ETc 150-280 mm as cover crop terminated at boot; 380-550 mm full grain; peak daily ETc 4.0-6.5 mm/day during jointing-heading.
evidence_registry.source_organization: FAO / Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education (SARE)
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration (FAO 56) & Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Allen, R.G. et al. (FAO) / Clark, A. (SARE)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cover crop rye uses 6-11 inches (150-280 mm) of water; rapid transpiration occurs during May jointing; WUE 1.8-2.8 kg/m3.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Measured across fall-seeded cover crop and grain trials.
evidence_registry.limitations: In semiarid western Corn Belt, late spring termination can deplete profile moisture for succeeding corn.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Root Architecture: Effective Water Extraction vs Maximum Anatomical Depth
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 90-120 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 150-210 cm in friable soils.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rye root system is extremely extensive and fibrous; effective active uptake concentrated in top 3-4 feet (90-120 cm); max penetration reaches 5-7 feet (150-210 cm).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep loess and silt loam prairie soils without shallow hardpans.
evidence_registry.limitations: Dense claypans (argillic horizons) restrict rooting to upper 60-90 cm.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Nutrient Uptake & Grain Nutrient Removal Standards
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Grain removal: 1.00 lb N/bu (17.9 kg N/t), 0.35 lb P2O5/bu (6.3 kg P2O5/t), 0.30 lb K2O/bu (5.4 kg K2O/t); Total uptake: 1.60 lb N/bu, 0.55 lb P2O5/bu, 1.45 lb K2O/bu.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Tri-State / Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station
evidence_registry.source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations (Bul. 974) & KSU Rye Nutrient Data
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Culman, S. et al. (Tri-State) / Mengel, D.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: At 50 bu/ac grain yield: rye exports 50 lb N, 17.5 lb P2O5, 15 lb K2O/acre in harvested grain.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: 56 lb/bu standard grain weight.
evidence_registry.limitations: Removal applies to grain harvest only; terminated cover crop exports 0.0 kg nutrients.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Slope
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 2.5-3.5 dS/m; yield decline slope 10.0% per dS/m; moderately tolerant.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rye exhibits moderate salt tolerance; initial yield threshold at EC_e 2.5-3.5 dS/m; superior to field beans but lower than barley.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Saturated soil paste electrical conductivity.
evidence_registry.limitations: Emergence stage is more sensitive to salinity than vegetative growth.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Cold Hardiness & Extreme Minimum Survival Temperature
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Survives down to -30 to -35°C under snow cover; -25°C bare soil; germination down to 1-2°C; lowest base temp (0.0-2.0°C) of all cereals.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Crop Science Society of America / Univ. of Saskatchewan
evidence_registry.source_title: Cold Acclimation and Low Temperature Tolerance of Cereal Crops
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Secale cereale exhibits the greatest cold hardiness of any temperate winter cereal; LT50 values of acclimated crowns reach -32°C to -34°C.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Gradual autumn cold acclimation with hardening photoperiod.
evidence_registry.limitations: Unacclimated rapid freeze shocks cause crown injury at higher temperatures (-12°C).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Heat Stress Sensitivity During Heading and Grain Filling
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 30.0-32.0°C; floret abortion and accelerated senescence occur above 32°C.
evidence_registry.source_title: Heat Unit Concepts and Stress in Small Grains
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Temperatures >86°F (30°C) during pollen shed cause floret sterility; temperatures >90°F (32°C) truncate grain filling.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: High solar radiation and low relative humidity.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cover crops terminated at boot avoid reproductive summer heat stress entirely.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Aboveground Biomass Production & Erosion Protection
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 3,000-6,500 kg/ha dry matter at boot to early heading; up to 8,000-10,000 kg/ha at maturity; reduces erosion by 60-90%.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cereal Rye Cover Crop and Water Quality in the Midwest
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Kaspar, T.C., Jaynes, D.B., Parkin, T.B., and Moorman, T.B.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rye cover crop produced 3.2 to 6.4 Mg/ha biomass; reduced rill and interrill soil erosion by 75-92% compared to no cover.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fall-seeded following corn or soybean harvest.
evidence_registry.limitations: Biomass varies dramatically with spring termination timing (1.5 Mg/ha at Feekes 4 vs 6.5 Mg/ha at Feekes 10.5).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Nitrate Scavenging Capacity & Groundwater Protection
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Scavenges 40-120 kg N/ha of residual fall soil nitrate; reduces subsurface drainage nitrate-N loss by 30-55%.
evidence_registry.source_title: Reducing Nitrate Leaching in the Corn Belt with Cereal Rye
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Cereal rye cover crop captured 48-115 kg N/ha, reducing annual flow-weighted tile nitrate concentrations by 42%.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Tile-drained silt loam and silty clay loam soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Captured nitrogen is recycled organically; not all is immediately plant-available to the next crop.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye C:N Ratio Progression, Stover Decomposition & Spring N Immobilization
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: C:N ratio 20:1-30:1 at jointing, 40:1-50:1 at boot, 65:1-85:1 at maturity; late termination immobilizes 20-40 lb N/ac.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Soil Science Society of America / USDA-ARS
evidence_registry.source_title: Time of Desiccation Effects on Plant Composition and Nitrogen Release from Rye
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Rye C:N increased from 24:1 in late March to 66:1 in late April; net N immobilization occurred for 4-8 weeks when C:N exceeded 35:1.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field decomposition in litterbags under no-till management.
evidence_registry.limitations: Successor corn requires starter N (20-40 lb N/ac) to offset early-season microbial tie-up.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Allelopathy: Benzoxazinoid Biosynthesis & Weed Suppression
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Synthesizes DIBOA and BOA in root exudates and shoots; suppresses small-seeded broadleaf weeds (pigweeds, waterhemp, lambsquarters).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Journal of Chemical Ecology / Michigan State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Role of Benzoxazinones in Allelopathy of Cereal Rye
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: DIBOA degrades to BOA in soil, exhibiting potent phytotoxicity against Amaranthus retroflexus and Chenopodium album; large-seeded crops are tolerant.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: High surface residue mulch under no-till.
evidence_registry.limitations: Allelopathy does not control established perennial weeds or large-seeded cocklebur/morningglory.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye to Corn Green Bridge & Seedling Pathogen Dynamics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Live rye roots harbor Pythium and Fusarium; requires 10-14 day termination window before corn planting to avoid seedling blight.
evidence_registry.source_organization: The American Phytopathological Society / Iowa State Univ.
evidence_registry.source_title: Green Bridge Dynamics and Corn Seedling Disease after Cereal Rye Termination
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Acharya, J., Bakker, M.G., Moorman, T.B., and Robertson, A.E.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Planting corn <7 days after rye termination increased Pythium root rot and decreased corn radicle length and emergence by 12-25%.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Cool, wet spring soils following glyphosate termination.
evidence_registry.limitations: Planting green is viable for soybean, but poses severe seedling disease risk for corn unless fungicide-treated and warm.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye-to-Soybean Rotational Synergy & Weed Suppression Performance
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; rye mulch suppresses Palmer amaranth and waterhemp; soybean fixes own N bypassing C:N immobilization.
evidence_registry.source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Univ. of Missouri / MCCC
evidence_registry.source_title: Cereal Rye Preceding Soybean: Agronomic and Economic Performance
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Soybean yields following cereal rye cover crop were equal to or greater than no-cover controls, while reducing herbicide inputs by 30%.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Commercial soybean varieties following winter rye
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Terminated at boot or early heading with roller-crimper or glyphosate.
evidence_registry.limitations: In drought years, excessive late rye growth can deplete seed zone moisture if not monitored.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Ploidy & Non-Vernalizing Habit of Common Oats
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Avena sativa L., Poaceae, allohexaploid (2n=6x=42), cool-season annual; vernalization not required for spring cultivars; 80-110 d grain.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database: Avena sativa L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Avena sativa L., common oat, cool-season annual grass; spring and winter biotypes; standard multi-purpose cereal.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard botanical classification.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring types dominate Midwest/Plains; winter types adapted only to USDA hardiness zones 7-9.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Oat Growth Stages & Growing Degree Day Accumulation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 4.4°C (40°F); cumulative GDD to grain maturity 1300-1700 GDD; 80-110 days active growth duration.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Minnesota Extension / NDSU Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Growing Oats in the Upper Midwest & Small Grain Phenology
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats require ~1400-1600 GDD (base 40°F) to mature; emergence occurs in 7-10 days at soil temps >40°F; heading occurs 50-60 d after emergence.
evidence_registry.geographic_scope: Northern Corn Belt & Northern Great Plains
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard spring seeding in April.
evidence_registry.limitations: Seeding past early May in the Midwest leads to severe yield and test weight reductions from summer heat.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Peak Daily Flux Rates
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 350-500 mm for grain, 150-250 mm for fall cover; peak daily water use 4.0-6.0 mm/day at heading.
evidence_registry.source_title: Yield Response to Water (FAO Irrigation Paper 33 & 56)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. / Allen, R.G. et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats seasonal water requirements vary from 350 to 500 mm; high transpiration coefficient (500-600 kg water/kg DM); peak ETc occurs during heading.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Rainfed and irrigated temperate production.
evidence_registry.limitations: Higher transpiration ratio than barley or wheat; more susceptible to late-season terminal drought.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Root Architecture: Effective Extraction Depth vs Maximum Penetration
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 70-100 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 120-150 cm; >75% of root mass in top 45 cm.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oat root system is fibrous and moderately deep; active uptake zone spans 2.5-3.5 feet (70-100 cm); max penetration reaches 4-5 feet (120-150 cm).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Unconstrained loam soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Root depth is shallower than winter rye or winter wheat.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Grain Removal Standards & Total Crop Nutrient Uptake
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Grain removal: 0.65 lb N/bu (18.6 kg N/t), 0.25 lb P2O5/bu (7.2 kg P2O5/t), 0.20 lb K2O/bu (5.7 kg K2O/t); Total uptake: 1.10 lb N/bu.
evidence_registry.source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations, Bulletin 974
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: At 80 bu/ac yield: oat grain exports 52 lb N, 20 lb P2O5, and 16 lb K2O per acre.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Commercial oats (32 lb/bu test weight standard)
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard 32 lb/bu grain bushel weight.
evidence_registry.limitations: Straw baling and removal exports an additional 25-35 lb K2O/acre.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Slope
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 3.0-4.0 dS/m; yield decline slope 10.0% per dS/m; moderately tolerant.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats maintain 100% relative yield up to EC_e 3.0 dS/m, with 50% yield reduction at EC_e 8.0 dS/m.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Electrical conductivity of saturated soil extract.
evidence_registry.limitations: More salt-tolerant than corn or soybean, but significantly less tolerant than barley.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Spring Oat Winter-Kill Threshold & Fall Cover Crop Termination Mechanism
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter-kills reliably at -7.0 to -9.0°C (15-20°F) consecutive freeze; zero spring chemical termination required.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cover Crops for Conservation Tillage Systems & Managing Cover Crops Profitably
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Spring oats planted in late summer will winterkill after several hard freezes (<20°F / -7°C), leaving a dead residue cover without spring regrowth.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fall seeding in August or early September.
evidence_registry.limitations: Winter-kill does not occur reliably in USDA zones 8-10, where oats survive winter as annual forage.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Thermal Sensitivity During Boot to Anthesis: Heat Breakpoint
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 28.0-30.0°C; temperatures >28°C during heading induce floret blasting and reduce test weight (<32 lb/bu).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Field Crops Research / MTT Agrifood Research
evidence_registry.source_title: Heat and Drought Sensitivity of Oats under Temperate Climates
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Peltonen-Sainio, P., Rajala, A., and Jauhiainen, L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats are exceptionally heat-sensitive; high temperatures (>28°C) between booting and grain filling reduced main shoot yield by up to 35% through floret blasting.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Controlled and field thermal stress treatments during heading.
evidence_registry.limitations: Fall cover crops avoid summer heat stress completely.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Fall Oat Cover Crop Biomass Accumulation & Soil Erosion Reduction
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 2,500-5,000 kg/ha dry matter in fall before winterkill; provides rapid 80-95% canopy cover within 40-50 days.
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably & Fall Cover Crop Trials
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats planted in August after small grain harvest produce 2 to 4 tons/acre dry matter before winter-kill, protecting soil from fall and spring erosion.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Spring oats used as cover crop
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Seeded before September 1 with adequate late summer rainfall.
evidence_registry.limitations: Seeding after September 15 in the Upper Midwest results in <1.0 ton/acre biomass due to thermal constraints.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oats as a Companion Nurse Crop for Perennial Legume Establishment
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Standard companion crop for alfalfa and red clover; suppresses weeds, protects soil, harvested at boot as oatlage or July as grain.
evidence_registry.source_title: Forage and Small Grain Establishment Guides, Extension Bulletin A2809
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Undersander, D., Cosgrove, D., and Cullen, E.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Seeding oats at 1.0-1.5 bu/acre with alfalfa prevents weed competition and wind erosion; early harvest at boot stage prevents lodging over alfalfa.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Co-seeded in early spring.
evidence_registry.limitations: Oats must be cut early (boot stage) in drought years to prevent excessive soil moisture competition with young alfalfa seedlings.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Winter-Killed Oat Residue C:N Dynamics & Rapid Spring Decomposition
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Residue C:N ratio 20:1-35:1 at freeze; decomposes rapidly in early spring; causes minimal spring N immobilization (<10 lb N/ac).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Canadian Journal of Soil Science / Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada
evidence_registry.source_title: Residue Decomposition and Nutrient Release of Annual Cereals
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Winter-killed vegetative oat residue has C:N of 25:1 to 32:1; cell walls rupture from freezing, facilitating rapid microbial breakdown in April.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field litterbag decomposition over winter and spring.
evidence_registry.limitations: Mature oat straw harvested for grain has higher C:N (45:1 to 60:1).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oat Sensitivity to Sulfonylurea and Triazine Herbicide Carryover
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Highly sensitive to atrazine, fomesafen, and sulfonylurea (e.g. chlorimuron) soil residues; plant-back interval 10-18 months.
evidence_registry.source_title: Illinois Weed Control Guide & Herbicide Carryover Tables
evidence_registry.citation_location: Illinois Agricultural Pest Management Handbook, Chapter 2
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oats are among the most sensitive small grains to atrazine carryover; requires 12-18 month rotational restriction if >1.5 lb ai/ac applied.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Soil pH >6.8 and low rainfall increase persistence.
evidence_registry.limitations: Check specific product master labels for regional rotational restrictions.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Winter-Killed Oats Preceding Corn: Clean Seedbed & Zero Green Bridge
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible predecessor to corn; leaves a mellow, friable seedbed with zero green bridge, no insect vectoring, and no soil drying.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Iowa State University Extension / Purdue Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Cover Crops for Modern Cropping Systems, PM 1714
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Winter-killed oats eliminate the green bridge risk for corn seedling diseases; soil warms faster than under living rye, supporting rapid corn emergence.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Oats completely winter-killed prior to spring.
evidence_registry.limitations: Provides less spring weed suppression than an overwintering rye cover crop.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: U.S. Commercial Oat Planting and Harvesting Date Windows Across Regions
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Midwest/Plains planting March 25 - April 30, harvest July 15 - August 20; Southern forage planting Sept 15 - Oct 31.
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Most active spring oat planting in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin, and North Dakota occurs in April; harvest peaks late July to early August.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Statistical 20-year survey distributions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Severe spring wetness can delay planting into May, reducing grain yields.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Ploidy & Perennial Longevity of Alfalfa
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Medicago sativa L., Fabaceae, autotetraploid (2n=4x=32), perennial forage legume; stand duration 3-5 yr (up to 7+ yr in West).
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database: Medicago sativa L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Medicago sativa L., alfalfa, perennial herbaceous legume; premier high-protein forage crop in North America.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard taxonomic classification.
evidence_registry.limitations: Stands thin naturally due to crown diseases and traffic after 4-6 years.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Multi-Cutting Phenology, Cutting Intervals & Fall Dormancy Classes
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 5.0°C; 3-5 cuttings/yr in Midwest, 6-8 in Southwest; 28-35 day cutting interval at early bud to 1/10 bloom; FD 1-11.
evidence_registry.source_organization: University of Wisconsin / Minnesota / Iowa State Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Alfalfa Management Guide (NCR 547)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Harvesting at bud to early bloom balances forage quality (crude protein 18-22%) with root carbohydrate replenishment; cumulative GDD 2200-3500/season.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard multi-harvest forage production.
evidence_registry.limitations: Frequent cutting before bud stage severely depletes crown carbohydrates, leading to stand death.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & High Irrigation Demand
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 600-1200 mm/yr; peak daily flux 6.0-9.0 mm/day; net irrigation requirement 400-900 mm in arid/semi-arid regions.
evidence_registry.source_organization: FAO / University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration (FAO 56) & Alfalfa Water Management (ANR Pub 8262)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Allen, R.G. et al. (FAO) / Hanson, B., Putnam, D., and Snyder, R.
evidence_registry.citation_location: UC ANR Publication 8262, pp. 1-12; FAO 56 Table 12
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa consumes 25-45 inches (630-1150 mm) of water per season depending on climate and cuttings; WUE 1.5-2.2 kg DM/m3.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fully irrigated western stands or full-season rainfed Midwest.
evidence_registry.limitations: One of the highest seasonal water-consuming field crops in North America.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Taproot Depth: Effective Extraction vs Maximum Bio-Drilling Depth
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 120-180 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 250-350 cm (documented up to 500-600 cm in deep alluvium).
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
evidence_registry.citation_location: NEH Part 652 Chapter 3; Weaver (1926) Chapter 18, pp. 215-240
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa possesses the deepest root system of any major field crop; taproots regularly penetrate 8-12 feet (250-350 cm); extreme penetration of 15-20 feet (500-600 cm) in deep loess.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Unconstrained deep soils without shallow bedrock or water tables.
evidence_registry.limitations: Acid subsoils (pH <5.5) or high water tables severely restrict taproot elongation.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Forage Nutrient Removal & Heavy Soil Potassium Depletion
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Forage removal: 50-65 lb N/ton (2.5-3.2% N), 12-15 lb P2O5/ton, 45-60 lb K2O/ton dry hay; massive potassium mining.
evidence_registry.source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations, Bulletin 974
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: A 5 ton/ac alfalfa hay yield removes ~280 lb N, 65 lb P2O5, and 250 lb K2O/acre annually, requiring aggressive potash management.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: 100% dry matter hay basis.
evidence_registry.limitations: Failure to apply potassium causes rapid stand thinning and winterkill.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Rate
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 2.0 dS/m; yield decline slope 7.3% per dS/m; moderately sensitive.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa yield is 100% up to EC_e 2.0 dS/m; decreases by 7.3% per dS/m above 2.0; 50% yield reduction at EC_e 8.9 dS/m.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Root-zone saturated paste extract conductivity.
evidence_registry.limitations: Seedling emergence stage is twice as sensitive to salinity as established plants.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Crown Freezing Tolerance & Critical Winter Survival Limits
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Air survival to -20 to -25°C under snow; lethal soil crown temperature -10 to -15°C (14 to 5°F) at 2-4 cm depth.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Science / Univ. of Wisconsin
evidence_registry.source_title: Freezing Resistance and Carbohydrate Composition in Alfalfa
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: McKenzie, J.S. et al. / Undersander, D.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crown temperatures below -12°C cause cellular membrane damage and winterkill; snow cover provides crucial thermal insulation.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Adequately acclimated crowns with high fall starch/fructan reserves.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cutting during the critical fall rest period (6 weeks prior to killing frost) increases winterkill risk.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa High Temperature Heat Stress & Summer Slump Phenomenon
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 32.0-35.0°C; night temps >20°C accelerate dark respiration, reducing forage yield and digestibility.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Environmental and Experimental Botany / Univ. of Minnesota
evidence_registry.source_title: Alfalfa Physiology and High Temperature Response
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Erice, G. et al. / Sheaffer, C.C.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Temperatures >32°C promote rapid stem lignification and reduce leaf-to-stem ratio; warm nights deplete nonstructural carbohydrates.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Midsummer field conditions under high solar radiation.
evidence_registry.limitations: Non-dormant southwestern cultivars tolerate higher temperatures than northern dormant types.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation by Sinorhizobium meliloti
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Sinorhizobium meliloti symbiosis; %Ndfa 70-90%; fixes 150-350 kg N/ha/yr (up to 400+ kg N/ha/yr in irrigated west).
evidence_registry.source_title: Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation in Alfalfa (Heichel et al. 1984 & Vance 2002)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Vance, C.P. / Heichel, G.H. et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa fixed 168 to 360 kg N/ha annually via 15N dilution; %Ndfa averaged 82% across diverse soil types.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Compatible Sinorhizobium meliloti nodulation at soil pH >6.5.
evidence_registry.limitations: Acid soils (pH <6.2) severely reduce nodule formation and nitrogenase enzyme activity.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Successor Fertilizer-N Credit to Corn: Year 1 and Year 2 Dynamics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: First-year N credit 100-150 lb N/ac (110-170 kg N/ha) to corn; second-year carryover credit 30-50 lb N/ac (35-55 kg N/ha).
evidence_registry.source_organization: Journal of Production Agriculture / Univ. of Wisconsin / Iowa State Univ.
evidence_registry.source_title: Fertilizer N Equivalence of Alfalfa for Succeeding Corn & Extension Guidelines
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Fox, R.H. and Piekielek, W.P. / Undersander, D. / Sawyer, J.
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Prod. Agric. 1:313-317; UW A2809; ISU PM 1714
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: First-year corn following terminated good alfalfa stand (>4 plants/ft2) requires zero to 40 lb N/ac starter, reflecting a 120-150 lb N/ac credit.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Good stand (>4 plants/ft2 or >50 stems/ft2) terminated in fall or spring.
evidence_registry.limitations: Poor stands (<2 plants/ft2) provide lower credits (60-80 lb N/ac); sandy soils experience rapid leaching.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Autotoxicity: Medicarpin Exudation & Rotational Break Requirement
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Medicarpin and phenolic root exudates inhibit seedling germination; requires 12-24 month rotational break before reseeding.
evidence_registry.source_title: Zone of Autotoxic Influence Around Established Alfalfa Plants
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Water-soluble autotoxic compounds from old alfalfa crowns reduce new seedling root growth by 60-80% within 8 inches (20 cm) of old plants.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Reseeding into terminated or thinned alfalfa fields.
evidence_registry.limitations: Interseeding into stands <1 year old is viable; stands >2 years old exhibit severe autotoxicity.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Strict Soil pH Sensitivity & Aluminum Toxicity Threshold
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 6.5-7.5; tolerated 6.0-8.0; below pH 6.2 Sinorhizobium nodulation fails and aluminum impairs taproot growth.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers / Univ. of Wisconsin Extension
evidence_registry.source_title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers (8th ed.) & Alfalfa Management Guide
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Havlin, J.L. et al. / Undersander, D. et al.
evidence_registry.citation_location: NCR 547 pp. 8-11; Havlin et al. Chapter 6
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa is highly sensitive to soil acidity; liming to pH 6.8 is required on acidic soils prior to establishment to ensure nodulation.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard agricultural soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Topsoil liming does not immediately neutralize acidic subsoils, which continue to impede deep taprooting.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa-to-Corn Rotational Synergies: Yield Premium & Rootworm Break
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; 10-15% corn yield premium over continuous corn; complete biological break for corn rootworm.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Univ. of Wisconsin
evidence_registry.source_title: Corn Rotational Response Following Alfalfa & NCR 547
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Camberato, J. and Nielsen, R.L. / Undersander, D.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: First-year corn following alfalfa yields 10-15% more than continuous corn even at non-limiting N fertilizer rates, due to soil structural improvements.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Alfalfa terminated in fall or early spring.
evidence_registry.limitations: Excessive early spring alfalfa growth must be terminated before it depletes topsoil moisture for corn emergence.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: U.S. Alfalfa Production Systems Across Midwest Dairy, Western Irrigated & Plains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Midwest/Northeast 3-5 cuttings rainfed; Western irrigated (CA, ID) 6-8+ cuttings; Northern Plains dryland 2-3 cuttings.
evidence_registry.source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook 628
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Alfalfa hay is harvested from May through October in the Midwest/Northeast, and March through November in California and Arizona.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Perennial alfalfa across all dormancy ratings
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Statistical 20-year survey distributions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Western systems depend almost entirely on irrigation water rights.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Climbing Habit & Cover Crop Role of Hairy Vetch
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Vicia villosa Roth, Fabaceae, diploid (2n=14), winter annual climbing legume; 210-270 d duration; premier winter cover crop.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database: Vicia villosa Roth
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vicia villosa Roth, hairy vetch, cool-season winter annual legume; high nitrogen-fixing capacity and climbing vine habit.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard taxonomic classification.
evidence_registry.limitations: Produces hard seed if allowed to mature, creating volunteer weed issues in small grains.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Phenology, Spring Biomass Surge & Optimal Termination Timing
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 4.0°C; 1100-1600 GDD to 50% bloom; optimal roller-crimper termination at 50-100% bloom (May); 210-270 d.
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hairy vetch accumulates >70% of its dry matter and fixed N during a 3-4 week surge in April-May; mechanical termination requires 50-100% bloom.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fall seeded in September; spring terminated in May.
evidence_registry.limitations: Premature termination (<50% bloom) leads to incomplete kill with roller-crimpers.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Biomass Production, Spring Soil Moisture Dynamics & Nitrogen Accumulation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass accumulation 3.0-5.5 Mg/ha; spring moisture extraction reaches 4.5-6.5 mm/day at flowering; rapid biomass accumulation provides substantial soil cover.
evidence_registry.source_title: Potential Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction through No-Till Cover-Crop Systems
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Teasdale, J.R., Coffman, C.B., and Mangum, R.W.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated hairy vetch biomass accumulation, nitrogen content, and spring soil water dynamics under no-till cover-crop systems, finding significant spring moisture depletion during late bloom.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field trials in Maryland on silt loam soils under rainfed no-till management.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring moisture depletion occurs primarily when termination is delayed into full bloom under low-rainfall conditions. FAO 56 crop coefficients provide generalized reference evapotranspiration multipliers.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Root Architecture: Effective Extraction vs Maximum Depth
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Branched taproot; effective water extraction depth 75-100 cm; maximum anatomical depth 120-150 cm; dense nodules in top 30 cm.
evidence_registry.source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vetch roots feature a distinct taproot with extensive lateral branches; active extraction concentrated in top 2.5-3.0 feet (75-100 cm); max depth 4-5 feet.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Permeable silt loam and sandy loam soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Waterlogged or compacted subsoils severely restrict lateral branching and nodule aeration.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Aboveground Biomass Accumulation & Tissue Nitrogen Content
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 3,000-6,000 kg/ha dry matter by 50% bloom; tissue nitrogen concentration 3.0-4.2% N (high succulent protein).
evidence_registry.source_title: Growth and Nitrogen Accumulation of Hairy Vetch Cover Crops
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hairy vetch produced 3.5 to 5.8 Mg/ha dry biomass containing 110 to 220 kg N/ha in aboveground shoots by mid-May.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Planted early September; terminated at full bloom in May.
evidence_registry.limitations: Early April termination yields <2.0 Mg/ha biomass and <60 kg N/ha.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Rate
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 1.5-2.5 dS/m; yield decline slope 12.0% per dS/m; moderately sensitive.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vetch is moderately sensitive to salinity; yields decline when EC_e exceeds 2.0 dS/m; nodulation is inhibited above 3.0 dS/m.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Root-zone saturated extract EC_e.
evidence_registry.limitations: Not suitable for saline-sodic soils in the semiarid West.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Winter Hardiness & Extreme Cold Survival Temperature
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Survives down to -15.0 to -20.0°C (0 to -4°F) with snow; base temperature 4.0°C; most winter-hardy annual legume in US.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Norwegian Journal of Agricultural Sciences / USDA-ARS
evidence_registry.source_title: Winter Survival of Hairy Vetch and Other Annual Legumes
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Brandsaeter, L.O. et al. / Teasdale, J.R.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hairy vetch is reliably winter-hardy in USDA hardiness zone 4 and warmer, withstanding -15°F (-26°C) under snow and -5°F (-20°C) bare ground.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Rosettes well-established with 4-6 leaves prior to freezing.
evidence_registry.limitations: Late-seeded small seedlings (<3 leaves) winterkill during severe bare-ground freezes.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Heat Stress Threshold & Late Spring Senescence
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 30.0-32.0°C; high temperatures in late spring accelerate senescence and terminate vegetative growth.
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably & Organic No-Till Trials
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vetch vegetative growth ceases when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 85°F (30°C); plants transition rapidly into pod filling and die.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Natural photoperiod and temperature transition in May-June.
evidence_registry.limitations: Requires termination before seed maturation to prevent weed problems.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation by Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viciae
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viciae; %Ndfa 70-85%; fixes 90-200 kg N/ha (80-180 lb N/ac); net soil N balance +90 to +200 kg N/ha.
evidence_registry.source_title: Nitrogen Fixation by Winter Cover Legumes
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Power, J.F., Doran, J.W., and Koerner, P.T.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hairy vetch fixed 112 to 215 kg N/ha via symbiotic fixation; 78-85% of total plant N was derived from atmospheric fixation.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Proper inoculation with Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viciae at seeding.
evidence_registry.limitations: High residual mineral soil N (>80 kg N/ha) depresses nodulation and fixation percentage.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Successor Fertilizer-N Credit to Corn and Sorghum
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Fertilizer replacement credit 60-120 lb N/ac (65-135 kg N/ha); directly reduces synthetic N fertilizer requirements for corn/sorghum.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cover Crop Nitrogen Contributions to Corn & Agronomy Facts 53
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Teasdale, J.R. et al. / Curran, W.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Agron. J. 96(6):1572-1581; Penn State Agronomy Facts 53
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Corn following hairy vetch achieved maximum yield with 80-120 lb/ac less synthetic fertilizer N than corn following fallow or small grains.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Terminated at 50-100% bloom in May with at least 3.0 Mg/ha biomass.
evidence_registry.limitations: Credit drops to 30-50 lb N/ac if terminated early (mid-April) due to reduced biomass accumulation.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch C:N Ratio & Explosive Spring Mineralization Kinetics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: C:N ratio 10:1-15:1; succulent tissue releases 50-75% of total nitrogen within 3-4 weeks post-termination; zero immobilization.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Soil Science Society of America Journal / North Carolina State Univ.
evidence_registry.source_title: Nitrogen Release from Crimson Clover and Hairy Vetch
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Vetch residue with C:N 11:1 mineralized rapidly, releasing 65% of shoot N in 28 days, perfectly synchronizing with corn V6-V12 demand.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Surface mulch or incorporated into warm spring soil (>15°C).
evidence_registry.limitations: Rapid N release can lead to leaching losses if heavy rainfall occurs before corn root establishment.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Roller-Crimper Termination Efficacy & Hard Seed Weed Risk in Small Grains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Mechanical roller-crimper requires 50-100% bloom for >90% kill; mature hard seed causes severe weed infestation in wheat/barley.
evidence_registry.source_title: Hairy Vetch Management for No-Till Organic Corn Production
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Roller-crimping at early bud yielded only 45% kill; crimping at late bloom achieved 93% kill; hard seed persists 2-5 years in soil.
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Hairy vetch in organic no-till systems
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: No-till chevron-pattern roller-crimper.
evidence_registry.limitations: Do not rotate hairy vetch before winter wheat or barley if any seed pods have matured.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Host Status for Root-Knot and Soybean Cyst Nematodes
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Susceptible reproductive host to Meloidogyne incognita and Heterodera glycines; caution before cotton, soybean, or tobacco.
evidence_registry.source_title: Evaluation of Winter Cover Crops as Hosts for Meloidogyne incognita
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Timper, P., Davis, R.F., and Tillman, P.G.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Hairy vetch supported high reproduction of Meloidogyne incognita (gall index 4.2), significantly increasing nematode pressure on succeeding cotton.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Sandy coastal plain soils with endemic nematode pressure.
evidence_registry.limitations: Do not plant hairy vetch in fields with active root-knot nematode infestations preceding susceptible cash crops.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch to Corn and Sorghum Rotational Synergies & Weed Mulch
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; provides 60-120 lb N/ac, thick in-situ residue mulch suppresses early weeds, boosts corn yield by 10-20%.
evidence_registry.source_title: Bio-Economic Evaluation of No-Till Corn Following Hairy Vetch
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Corn planted into rolled or desiccated hairy vetch mulch outyielded bare-ground no-till controls by 15% and reduced early weed emergence by 78%.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: No-till planter equipped with heavy-duty coulters and row cleaners.
evidence_registry.limitations: Vetch vines can wrap around planter wheels if not properly rolled or chemically desiccated.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Botanical Identity, Morphology & Functional Classification
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Trifolium incarnatum L. (TRIN3); Fabaceae; erect annual bunchgrass-like legume (0.3-0.8 m); dark green pilose trifoliolate leaves; elongated scarlet conical flower heads (2.5-6.0 cm); non-stoloniferous.
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database — Trifolium incarnatum L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Trifolium incarnatum L. is an introduced winter annual legume widely cultivated across the Southeastern and Mid-Atlantic United States for forage, green manure, soil cover, and pollinator support.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard taxonomic description and growth habit profile.
evidence_registry.limitations: Taxonomic baseline; morphological height and tiller development vary with seeding density and spring temperature.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Phenology, Thermal Base & Growing Degree Day Accumulation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth 180-240 days (winter annual) or 60-90 days (spring-seeded north); base temperature 4.0-5.0°C; 1000-1500 GDD accumulated to full bloom.
evidence_registry.source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crimson clover grows rapidly in autumn, remains semi-dormant during mid-winter freezes, and resumes vigorous growth in early spring, flowering earlier than hairy vetch or red clover.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Fall seeded in late August to October depending on latitude.
evidence_registry.limitations: GDD accumulation varies by planting date and cultivar dormancy characteristics.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Cold Hardiness, Winter Survival Limits & Frost-Heaving Dynamics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Absolute minimum survival -12°C to -15°C (10°F to 5°F) with snow cover; winter-kills below -15°C to -18°C on bare soil; vulnerable to freeze-thaw frost-heaving.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Midwest Cover Crops Council
evidence_registry.source_title: Crimson Clover Cover Crop for Midwestern Systems
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Midwest Cover Crops Council / Purdue Extension
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crimson clover reliably overwinters in USDA Zone 6b and south. In Zone 5 and north, lack of continuous snow cover or severe midwinter temperature drops result in stand winter-kill and crown frost-heaving on heavy soils.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Established rosette with >=4-6 true leaves before first killing frost.
evidence_registry.limitations: Late-planted clover with <4 leaves suffers 100% winter-kill below -10°C.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Soil Moisture Depletion
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 250-400 mm; peak daily water use 3.5-5.5 mm/day during late vegetative and bloom stages in April-May; moderate-to-low drought tolerance.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration: Guidelines for Computing Crop Water Requirements
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., and Smith, M.
evidence_registry.citation_location: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 12
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Clover cover crop Kc values range from 0.4 in early vegetative stage to 1.05-1.15 at full bloom, drawing 3.5-5.5 mm/day from the upper 60 cm soil profile.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Well-watered reference conditions; termination timing strongly modulates total moisture extraction.
evidence_registry.limitations: Delayed spring termination in dry years desiccates seedbed for subsequent corn or cotton.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Soil pH Boundaries, Acidity Sensitivity & Salinity Threshold
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal soil pH 6.0-7.0 (tolerates 5.5-7.5); highly sensitive to aluminum toxicity at pH <5.2; sensitive to salinity (ECe threshold 1.5-2.0 dS/m).
evidence_registry.source_organization: U.S. Salinity Laboratory / John Wiley & Sons
evidence_registry.source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance — Current Assessment & Soil Fertility Management
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Havlin, J.L. et al.
evidence_registry.citation_location: ASCE J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103(2):115-134; Soil Fertility and Fertilizers 8th ed.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crimson clover nodulation and root elongation decline sharply below pH 5.5 due to aluminum and manganese toxicity. It is classified as sensitive to soil salinity with yield reductions beginning above 1.5 dS/m.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Saturated soil paste extract (ECe) electrical conductivity measurement.
evidence_registry.limitations: Liming strongly improves nodulation on acid Southeastern ultisols.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Root System Architecture & Effective Water Extraction Depth
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Branched fibrous taproot; effective water extraction depth 40-70 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 80-120 cm; low-to-moderate compaction alleviation.
evidence_registry.source_title: Root Development of Field Crops & National Engineering Handbook Part 652
evidence_registry.citation_location: Root Development of Field Crops, Chapter 19; NEH Part 652, Table 3-4
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crimson clover produces a distinct taproot with extensive lateral branches concentrated in the upper 40-60 cm of soil, rarely penetrating subsoil hardpans beyond 100-120 cm.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep permeable agricultural soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Root depth is severely restricted by dense subsoil fragipans or high water tables.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Symbiotic Biological Nitrogen Fixation & Rhizobium Specificity
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Symbiont: Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. trifolii (Type R); fixes 70-150 kg N/ha (60-135 lb N/ac); 60-80% Ndfa under optimal nodulation.
evidence_registry.source_organization: North Carolina State University Extension / SARE
evidence_registry.source_title: Winter Annual Legumes for Conservation Tillage
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Ranells, N.N., Wagger, M.G., and Hoyt, G.D.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Inoculated crimson clover fixes between 70 and 150 kg N/ha, deriving 60% to 80% of its total nitrogen from the atmosphere through symbiosis with R. leguminosarum bv. trifolii.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Effective inoculation with fresh clover-specific Rhizobium inoculant on soils with low residual N.
evidence_registry.limitations: High soil nitrate levels (>25 ppm) suppress nodulation and reduce %Ndfa.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Biomass Yield, Tissue N Concentration & C:N Decomposition Kinetics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Dry matter biomass 2,500-5,500 kg/ha; tissue N concentration 2.5-3.8%; C:N ratio 12:1 to 18:1; rapid residue mineralization releasing 50% N in 3-5 weeks.
evidence_registry.source_title: Nitrogen Release from Crimson Clover in Relation to Plant Maturity and Decomposition
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated decomposition and N release of crimson clover terminated at late vegetative through full bloom, finding rapid decomposition with net mineralization beginning immediately due to low C:N ratio (12:1 to 17:1).
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field litterbag incubation on sandy loam and clay loam soils under conservation tillage.
evidence_registry.limitations: Delaying termination to late seed maturity increases C:N ratio to >22:1, slowing decomposition.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Rotational Nitrogen Replacement Credit to Succeeding Cash Crops
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Fertilizer-N replacement credit 40-80 lb N/ac (45-90 kg N/ha) to corn, sorghum, or cotton; zero microbial N immobilization; rapid early mineralization.
evidence_registry.source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Auburn University
evidence_registry.source_title: Review of Fertilizer Nitrogen Credits for Crimson Clover in Conservation Tillage
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Torbert, H.A., Reeves, D.W., and Mulvaney, R.L.
evidence_registry.citation_location: J. Prod. Agric. 9(1):95-100; Auburn Ext. Circular ANR-1311
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Across multi-year trials in the Southeast, crimson clover replaced 40 to 80 lb/ac of commercial synthetic nitrogen fertilizer for following corn and cotton crops without causing stover nitrogen immobilization.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Terminated at 50% to full bloom and incorporated or left as no-till surface mulch.
evidence_registry.limitations: Credit declines to 20-30 lb N/ac if clover stand is sparse (<50% ground cover) or terminated prematurely.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Mechanical Termination via Roller-Crimper & Regrowth Constraints
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Roller-crimper termination requires >=75-100% full bloom for complete kill; rolling at vegetative or early bud stage results in 40-60% regrowth.
evidence_registry.source_title: Hairy Vetch and Crimson Clover Management for No-Till Organic Corn
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Mischler, R.A., Duiker, S.W., Curran, W.S., and Wilson, D.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Crimson clover rolling efficacy is tightly correlated with physiological bloom stage; full floral elongation and early senescence are necessary for permanent roller-crimper termination without chemical herbicides.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Evaluated using chevron-blade roller-crimper on no-till organic field sites.
evidence_registry.limitations: In conventional systems, glyphosate or 2,4-D/dicamba burndown allows earlier vegetative termination.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Soil Coverage, Erosion Control & Aggregate Stabilization
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Rapid canopy closure provides 85-98% ground cover by mid-spring; reduces rainfall runoff by 40-65% and sediment erosion by 60-80% compared to winter fallow.
evidence_registry.source_title: Restoration of Degraded Soils with Cover Crops in the Southeastern USA
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Langdale, G.W., Blevins, R.L., Karlen, D.L., et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated long-term soil conservation effects of winter legume cover crops, showing crimson clover significantly improved soil organic carbon, aggregate stability, and reduced soil loss on sloping terrain.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Rainfed conservation tillage systems on sandy loam ultisols.
evidence_registry.limitations: Slow early-autumn growth on late-planted fields leaves soil vulnerable to early-winter sheet erosion.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Host Status for Nematodes, Crown Rot Pathogens & Corn Rootworm Break
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Non-host biological break for Corn Rootworm; host to Meloidogyne incognita (Southern Root-Knot Nematode) and Sclerotinia trifoliorum (clover rot); weak host to SCN.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Organization of Nematologists of Tropical America (ONTA)
evidence_registry.source_title: Evaluation of Cover Crops as Hosts for Root-Knot Nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.)
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Timper, P., Davis, R.F., and Tillotson, D.K.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Demonstrated that crimson clover is a moderate-to-good host for Meloidogyne incognita, which can multiply nematode populations preceding susceptible cotton or vegetable crops.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Greenhouse and microplot nematode reproduction factor assays.
evidence_registry.limitations: In cold-winter northern zones, low soil temperatures suppress winter nematode reproduction.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Rotational Synergies with Corn, Sorghum & Cotton
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Supplies 40-80 lb N/ac and 8-14% yield premium to subsequent corn and cotton in conservation tillage; breaks grass disease cycles.
evidence_registry.source_title: Cover Crops and Rotations for Conservation Tillage Systems
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Reviewed conservation tillage systems, documenting that winter legume cover crops, particularly crimson clover, consistently increased succeeding corn and cotton yields over winter fallow across diverse soils.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Long-term conservation tillage research comparisons.
evidence_registry.limitations: Spring moisture depletion requires timely termination in sub-humid production regions.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Regional Adaptation, Hardiness Zones & Reseeding Management
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Premier winter annual cover crop across USDA Zones 6b-9; adapted to Coastal Plain, Piedmont, Mid-South, and Ohio Valley; summer annual in Zone 4-5.
evidence_registry.source_title: Crimson Clover in Conservation Tillage Systems
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Hancock, D.W., Durham, R.G., and Cabrera, M.L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Details regional management guidelines for crimson clover in the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic, highlighting cultivar selection for hard seed production (Dixie) versus early maturity (AU Robin).
evidence_registry.variety_scope: Dixie, AU Robin, AU Sunrise, Tibbee
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field management guide based on university field trials.
evidence_registry.limitations: Reseeding cultivars create volunteer weed risks in subsequent winter small grain crops.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Botanical Identity, Brassicaceae Classification & Non-Fixing Habit
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Raphanus sativus L. (RASA2); Brassicaceae; cool-season annual; basal rosette of lyrate leaves with swollen cylindrical taproot (15-35 cm); non-legume (0.0 kg N/ha BNF).
evidence_registry.source_title: The PLANTS Database — Raphanus sativus L.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Raphanus sativus L. is an annual brassica cultivated as an agricultural cover crop (tillage/forage radish) for soil compaction alleviation, nutrient capture, and weed suppression.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard taxonomic description and growth form catalog.
evidence_registry.limitations: Cultivars selected for cover cropping (daikon/oilseed) differ from culinary radishes in taproot elongation and glucosinolate profile.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Phenology, Thermal Base & Rapid Autumn Growth Cycle
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth duration 50-75 days (late summer to winter-kill); base temperature 3.0-4.0°C; 600-1000 GDD accumulated; photoperiod bolting sensitivity.
evidence_registry.source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Michigan State University
evidence_registry.source_title: Evaluating Cover Crops for Benefits, Costs and Performance within Diverse Cropping Systems
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Snapp, S.S., Date, K., and Kirk, W.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Oilseed radish establishes extraordinarily rapidly in August-September, accumulating significant canopy and taproot biomass in 6-8 weeks before mid-winter termination.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Late summer seeding following small grain or early vegetable harvest.
evidence_registry.limitations: Early summer seedings bolt prematurely in response to long days, producing woody stalks and reduced fleshy taproots.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Winter-Kill Temperature Thresholds & Complete Biomass Collapse
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Winter-kills reliably at sustained temperatures below -6°C to -9°C (21°F to 15°F) for >=4-6 hours; cellular ice crystallization causes complete root collapse.
evidence_registry.source_title: Thinking about Cover Crops? Think Radish
evidence_registry.citation_location: UMD Extension Fact Sheet FS-824, pp. 1-6
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Forage radish winter-kills completely in the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest when temperatures fall into the teens (<= -7°C) for several consecutive nights, eliminating the need for spring herbicide or mechanical termination.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Vegetative fleshy taproots with high water content (>90%).
evidence_registry.limitations: In USDA Zones 8-9 (Deep South/California), mild winters prevent reliable winter-kill, requiring chemical burndown.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Subsoil Compaction Alleviation & Bio-Drilling Macropore Formation
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Thick fleshy taproot penetrates compacted subsoil layers (>2.0 MPa penetration resistance); winter decay creates open vertical macropores (2-5 cm wide, 1-2 m deep).
evidence_registry.source_title: Penetration of Compact Subsoils by Diverse Cover Crop Roots
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated root growth of forage radish, rye, and rapeseed in compacted soils, demonstrating radish roots had significantly higher penetration density in compacted subsoils (>2.0 MPa) than rye or rapeseed, creating biopores used by subsequent corn roots.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field and rhizotron experiments across silt loam and sandy loam soils with induced plow pans.
evidence_registry.limitations: Compaction alleviation fails if soil is severely smeared, waterlogged, or if planting is delayed (<40 days of growth before freeze).

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Infiltration Enhancement
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 150-300 mm over 60-day autumn window; peak daily water use 3.0-4.5 mm/day; winter-decay biopores increase water infiltration rates 2-3 fold.
evidence_registry.source_title: Root Growth and Yield of Maize as Affected by Previous Cover Crops and Soil Compaction
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Documented that forage radish taproot biopores dramatically improved saturated hydraulic conductivity and deep water infiltration, reducing surface runoff and enhancing subsoil water recharge.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Measurements conducted on no-till maize fields following winter-killed cover crops.
evidence_registry.limitations: Infiltration increases (2- to 3-fold) were measured in Maryland silt loam soils via constant-head permeameters in open winter-decay biopores (Chen & Weil 2011); benefit depends on presence of dense plow pan and uncollapsed biopores; rapid autumn water extraction can dry topsoil during droughty autumns.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Soil pH Preferences, Salinity Tolerance & Waterlogging Sensitivity
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal soil pH 6.0-7.5 (tolerates 5.5-8.0); moderately tolerant to salinity (ECe threshold 3.0-4.0 dS/m); poor waterlogging tolerance (rots in standing water).
evidence_registry.source_title: Tolerance of Vegetable and Brassica Crops to Salinity
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Raphanus sativus exhibits moderate salinity tolerance with a yield decline threshold around 3.5 dS/m, but fleshy taproots are highly prone to soft rot (Erwinia/Pectobacterium) in ponded or anaerobic soils.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard salinity tank and field drainage trials.
evidence_registry.limitations: Waterlogged clay soils result in stunted, unbranched, rotting taproots.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Fleshy Taproot Dimensions & Deep Anatomical Penetration
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Fleshy storage root 15-35 cm length, 2.5-7.0 cm diameter; fine vertical taproot penetrates 150-240 cm (5-8 ft); effective extraction depth 60-120 cm.
evidence_registry.source_title: Root Development of Field Crops & Field Soil Studies
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Weaver, J.E. / Chen, G. and Weil, R.R.
evidence_registry.citation_location: Root Development of Field Crops, Chapter 22; Soil & Tillage Res. 108:31-40
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: The enlarged fleshy upper taproot is accompanied by a slender vertical taproot that extends rapidly into the deep subsoil, documented to depths of 1.5 to 2.4 m in unconstrained loess and coastal plain soils.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Deep uncompacted or macropore-rich soil profiles.
evidence_registry.limitations: Extreme compaction (>3.5 MPa) restricts root elongation, forcing horizontal swelling.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Residual Nitrate Scavenging Capacity & Profile Recovery
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Exceptional autumn nitrate scavenger, capturing 100-220 kg N/ha (100-200 lb N/ac) from soil profile; reduces nitrate leaching to groundwater by 60-90%.
evidence_registry.source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Soil Science Society of America
evidence_registry.source_title: Brassica Cover Crops for Nitrogen Scavenging in the Mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated N uptake by forage radish, showing it accumulated 110 to 220 kg N/ha in aboveground and belowground biomass, significantly depleting soil profile nitrate down to 1.5 m compared to winter fallow or rye.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Planted in late August following heavily fertilized sweet corn and field corn.
evidence_registry.limitations: Total N scavenged depends strictly on available soil residual mineral N.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Biomass Yield, C:N Quality & Rapid Spring Decomposition
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Total dry matter 4,500-9,000 kg/ha (top: 3,000-6,000; root: 1,500-3,500); low C:N ratio (10:1 to 15:1); succulent tissue decomposes rapidly upon freezing.
evidence_registry.source_title: Nitrogen Release Dynamics from Brassica Cover Crops
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Jahanzad, E., Barker, A.V., Hashemi, M., et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Demonstrated that forage radish tissues possess narrow C:N ratios (9:1 to 13:1 for leaves, 12:1 to 16:1 for fleshy roots) and low lignin, resulting in explosive microbial decomposition upon winter thaw.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Field litterbag and mineral N extraction trials under temperate winter conditions.
evidence_registry.limitations: Rapid breakdown emits strong sulfurous/mercaptan odors in late winter.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Spring Nitrogen Release Kinetics & Leaching Vulnerability
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Releases 70-80% of captured N in March-April; on coarse sandy soils, early mineralized nitrate can leach before May corn uptake unless captured by companion grass.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Soil Science Society of America / University of California
evidence_registry.source_title: Tillage and Cover Crop Effects on Nitrogen Mineralization and Leaching Dynamics
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Veenstra, J.J., Horwath, W.R., and Mitchell, J.P.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Showed that rapid nitrogen release from winter-killed brassica cover crops in early spring creates a temporal asynchrony with summer annual crop demand, leading to leaching on permeable sandy profiles without companion winter cereals.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Lysimeter and soil core mineralization assays.
evidence_registry.limitations: Pairing radish with cereal rye effectively prevents early-spring nitrate loss.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Glucosinolates & Biofumigation Suppression of Soil Pathogens
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: High glucosinolate content (4-methylthio-3-butenyl glucosinolate); enzymatic hydrolysis produces isothiocyanates (ITCs) that suppress soil fungi and nematodes.
evidence_registry.source_organization: CSIRO Plant Industry / Kluwer Academic Publishers
evidence_registry.source_title: Biofumigation Potential of Brassicas: Glucosinolate Profiles and Biological Activity
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Quantified glucosinolate concentrations across brassica roots and shoots, finding Raphanus sativus produced high levels of biologically active sulfur compounds capable of suppressing Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Verticillium in vitro.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Laboratory gas chromatography and fungal bioassays.
evidence_registry.limitations: Glucosinolate biofumigation is a secondary, variable biological suppression mechanism observed primarily in vitro and in closed microplots (Kirkegaard & Sarwar 1998); natural winter-kill tissue release is diffuse and does not substitute for commercial fungicides or nematicides.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Pest Vulnerabilities, Clubroot Risk & Nematode Break
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Susceptible to Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae), flea beetles, and cabbage looper; non-host biological break for Soybean Cyst Nematode (SCN).
evidence_registry.source_title: Potential of Brassicaceous Cover Crops for Nematode Management
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Melakeberhan, H., Mennan, S., Chen, S., et al.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Evaluated oilseed radish across multiple nematode species, showing it is a non-host to Heterodera glycines (SCN) and suppresses Pratylenchus penetrans, but can amplify brassica-specific pathogens if rotated with brassica vegetables.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Nematode reproduction factor assays across sandy loam field soils.
evidence_registry.limitations: Susceptible host to Clubroot and flea beetles; non-host break for SCN (Melakeberhan et al. 2010). Caution is warranted when rotating with commercial brassicas (canola, broccoli, cabbage) in fields with Clubroot history or acidic soils (pH <6.8); requires 3- to 4-year rotational breaks and pH management rather than representing an automatic statutory prohibition.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Rotational Synergies with Corn, Soybean & Small Grains
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Precedes corn and soybean with 5-10% yield bump on compacted soils; ideal after winter wheat/barley; requires high caution preceding commercial brassicas due to shared Clubroot risk; creates mellow seedbed.
evidence_registry.source_title: Oilseed Radish: A Versatile Cover Crop for Michigan
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Provides comprehensive rotational guidelines: wheat-radish-corn rotation provides optimal timing; winter-kill eliminates spring tillage; improves early corn rooting and drought resilience.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Standard multi-crop field rotations in conservation tillage.
evidence_registry.limitations: Corn yield increase (5-10%) is conditional on compacted no-till soils where radish biopores relieve subsoil physical impedance (Chen & Weil 2011; MSU E-3165); response is negligible on loose uncompacted soils. Requires planting within 1-2 weeks of wheat/barley harvest (August) for maximum root mass.

evidence_registry.attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Rapid Canopy Closure, Weed Suppression & Odor Dynamics
evidence_registry.recorded_value_or_summary: Achieves 100% canopy cover in 3-4 weeks; suppresses fall and early-spring winter annual weeds (marestail, chickweed); sulfurous decay odor during spring thaw.
evidence_registry.source_organization: Weed Science Society of America / USDA-ARS
evidence_registry.source_title: Forage Radish Cover Crop Suppresses Winter Annual Weeds in Fall and Early Spring
evidence_registry.author_or_institution: Lawley, Y.E., Weil, R.R., and Teasdale, J.R.
evidence_registry.exact_supporting_context: Demonstrated that forage radish provided near-complete suppression of winter annual weeds in autumn and through early April, mediated by rapid light interception and release of allelopathic glucosinolates.
evidence_registry.conditions_and_assumptions: Seeded at 6-10 lb/acre in late August under conservation tillage.
evidence_registry.limitations: Weed suppression declines rapidly by late April as radish residue decomposes completely.
